# The Good Samaritan: Being Kind to Everyone

**Let me ask you something:** Imagine you're walking home from school, and you see someone sitting alone on the curb, looking sad. They're not your friend. You don't know them very well. They're just... there. What would you do? Would you stop? Would you help? Or would you keep walking?

That's the question we're exploring today, and it's one that Jesus asked people about too—a long, long time ago.

---

**Here's the story:**

Once upon a time, a man was walking down a dusty road. It was hot. Really hot. The sun was beating down, and he was probably thinking about getting home, having a cool drink, maybe sitting in the shade.

But then—oh no!—bandits jumped out and robbed him. They took everything. His money, his bag, his sandals. They even hurt him pretty badly and left him lying on the side of the road, groaning and bleeding.

Now, a priest came walking down that same road. A priest! Someone really important and religious. You'd think he'd help, right? But he saw the hurt man and... he crossed to the other side of the road and walked right past. Maybe he was in a hurry. Maybe he was scared. Maybe he thought, *That's not my problem.*

Then a temple helper came along. Another person who worked in God's house! Surely *he'd* help? But no—he also looked at the hurt man, crossed to the other side, and kept walking.

The poor man was still lying there, hurt and alone.

**Then came someone nobody expected.**

A Samaritan came walking down the road. Now, here's the important part: Jewish people and Samaritans didn't like each other. Not one bit. They were enemies. They didn't hang out together. They didn't help each other.

But when this Samaritan saw the hurt man, something amazing happened.

He stopped.

He knelt down beside the stranger. He cleaned the man's wounds with oil and wine. He wrapped them up carefully. He didn't say, "That's gross," or "That's not my job." He just... helped. Then he put the hurt man on his own donkey, took him to an inn, and paid the innkeeper to take care of him.

**Do you see what makes this so special?**

The Samaritan didn't help because the man was his friend. He didn't help because they were the same. He helped because someone needed help—and that was enough.

The priest and the temple helper walked past. But the Samaritan? He crossed the road *toward* the hurt man, not away from him.

---

**So what does this mean for us?**

Kindness isn't just about being nice to your best friends or your family. Real kindness means helping people even when:

- They're different from you
- You don't know them very well
- Nobody's watching
- It's messy or inconvenient
- You might get your clothes dirty

The Samaritan got his hands dirty. He spent his own money. He took time out of his day. But he did it anyway.

**And here's the beautiful part:** Jesus told this story and said, "Go and do the same."

He wasn't just talking about helping people on dusty roads. He was saying: *Be kind to everyone. Don't walk past people who need help. Be a Good Samaritan.*

---

**This week, I want you to try something:**

Look around. Really look. Is there someone at school who's sitting alone? Someone who doesn't have many friends? Someone who looks sad or left out? 

That's your moment. That's when you can be a Good Samaritan.

Maybe you sit with them at lunch. Maybe you ask them to play. Maybe you just say hello and smile. It doesn't have to be big. It just has to be kind.

You don't need to be a superhero. You just need to notice, care, and act.

That's what the Good Samaritan did.

That's what *you* can do.

# The Good Samaritan: Being Kind to Everyone

**Have you ever helped someone when it was actually kind of hard to do?**

Maybe you shared your toy with someone who wasn't even your friend. Or you included someone at lunch who usually sits alone. Or you helped your little brother even though you really wanted to play outside instead.

Well, today I want to tell you a story that Jesus told a long, long time ago. It's about someone who did something really, really kind—even though it was difficult. And the cool part? It's still teaching us how to be good friends today.

## The Story

Picture this: A man is walking down a dusty road. The sun is hot. He's minding his own business, just going about his day. Then—*uh oh*—some robbers jump out! They take his money, tear his clothes, and leave him lying on the side of the road, hurt and scared. He can't get up. He needs help *badly*.

Soon, another man comes walking down the same road. This man is important—he works at the temple. You'd think he'd help, right? But no. He sees the hurt man, and he... walks right past. Maybe he was in a hurry. Maybe he was worried. Maybe he thought, *That's not my problem.* And he just kept walking.

Then another man comes along. This one is also important. But he does the same thing—he looks, and then he walks right past too.

**Now here comes the surprising part.**

The next person to walk down that road is a Samaritan. And here's the thing: the Jewish people (like the hurt man) didn't like Samaritans. They thought they were different. They didn't treat them as friends. They didn't even say hello to them usually.

But this Samaritan? When he saw the hurt man, his heart filled with love. He didn't think, *Oh, he's not my friend. He's not my family. He's not like me.* 

Instead, he stopped.

He cleaned the man's wounds with oil and wine. He wrapped him up carefully. He put him on his own donkey and took him to an inn—a place where people could rest and get better. He paid the innkeeper to look after him. He said, "Take care of him. If you spend more money than this, I'll pay you back when I come again."

**That's real kindness.**

## Why Was This So Special?

The Samaritan didn't have to help. He didn't know this man. They weren't friends. In fact, they were supposed to be *enemies*. But he helped anyway because he saw someone who was hurting, and he cared.

Jesus told this story to teach us something important: **Being kind doesn't mean only being nice to your friends. Real kindness means helping *anyone* who needs help—even if they're different from you, even if they don't go to your school, even if you've never met them before.**

The two important men who walked past? They only cared about people like themselves. But the Samaritan? He saw a person in trouble, and that was enough.

## Your Turn

Here's what I want you to think about this week:

**Who is someone you could be a "Good Samaritan" to?**

Maybe it's the kid who sits alone at lunch. Maybe it's someone new at school who doesn't have many friends yet. Maybe it's someone your friends don't like—but they need kindness anyway. Maybe it's someone in your neighborhood, or someone in your family who's having a hard time.

You don't have to do something huge. You could:
- Say hello and smile
- Include them in a game
- Share your snack
- Help them when they're confused about something
- Sit with them when they look lonely

The Good Samaritan didn't wait to be asked. He didn't need a reward. He just *saw* someone who needed help and he *did* something about it.

**That can be you.**

This week, be on the lookout for someone who needs a little kindness. And then be brave enough to give it—just like the Good Samaritan.

# The One Who Stopped

Hey everyone! I want you to imagine something with me.

You're at the playground. You don't know anyone there. And then you see a kid sitting by the swings, all alone, crying. They've fallen off and scraped their knee pretty badly. Blood is trickling down their shin. Their lip is wobbling.

Here's my question: **What would you do?**

Would you run over and help? Would you walk past and keep playing? Would you go find a grown-up?

Hold that thought. Because Jesus once told a story about exactly this kind of moment. And it's one of the best stories ever told.

---

One day, a man was walking down a long, dusty road from Jerusalem to a city called Jericho. It was a lonely road. Rocky. Winding through hills and shadows. The kind of road where you walk a little faster because it feels spooky.

And then — the worst thing happened.

Robbers jumped out. They grabbed him. They took everything he had — his money, his coat, even his shoes. Then they beat him up and left him lying in the dirt, hurt so badly he couldn't even stand. He just lay there, groaning, hoping — *praying* — that someone would come along and help.

And guess what? Someone did come along!

A priest walked down that same road. Now, a priest was an important religious leader. Someone everyone respected. Someone who taught people about God and about being good. If *anyone* was going to help, surely it would be him.

The priest saw the man lying there. Bleeding. Barely moving.

And he crossed to the other side of the road. And kept walking.

Gone.

Can you believe that? I know. It's shocking.

But wait — here comes someone else! A Levite. That's another important person from the temple. He also knew all about God's rules, including the rule that says love your neighbour.

The Levite walked closer. He actually *looked* at the man. He could see the cuts and bruises. He could hear him whimpering.

And then he crossed to the other side too. And kept walking.

Gone.

Two people who *should* have helped. Two people who knew better. And neither one stopped.

Now. Here comes the surprising part.

A Samaritan came down the road.

And here's what you need to know: in those days, the Jewish people and the Samaritan people did *not* get along. At all. They avoided each other. They wouldn't eat together, wouldn't talk to each other, wouldn't even walk through each other's towns. If you'd asked the hurt man before all this happened, "Who's the last person you'd want help from?" he might have said, "A Samaritan."

But this Samaritan saw the man lying in the road, and his heart broke.

He didn't cross to the other side. He didn't look away. He didn't think, "Well, he's not *my* kind of person."

He ran over. He knelt down in the dirt. He poured cool oil and wine on the man's wounds — that was like medicine back then — and it stung, but it would help him heal. He tore strips of cloth and carefully wrapped every cut. He talked to the man gently. He lifted him up — carefully, slowly — and set him on his own donkey.

Then he *walked* so the hurt man could *ride*.

He brought him to an inn — kind of like a hotel — and took care of him all night long. And the next morning, when the Samaritan had to leave, he gave the innkeeper his own money and said, "Look after him. Whatever it costs, I'll pay you back."

---

Isn't that amazing?

The people who were *supposed* to help didn't. The person nobody *expected* to help did everything.

Jesus told this story and then asked a simple question: **"Which one was a real neighbour?"**

And the answer was obvious. The one who stopped. The one who was kind. Not the one who knew the right things, but the one who *did* the right thing.

Here's what I want you to remember:

**Kindness doesn't check who someone is before it helps.**

It doesn't matter if someone is your best friend or a total stranger. It doesn't matter if they look like you, talk like you, or like the same things you do. When someone is hurting, you can be the one who stops.

---

So here's your challenge this week. Just one thing.

Find someone who isn't in your friend group — maybe someone sitting alone at lunch, or a kid who looks left out at break time — and do one kind thing for them. Sit with them. Ask their name. Share your snack. Just *stop* for them.

You might be the only person who does.

And that? That makes you a Good Samaritan.

Now go be amazing. I know you will. 💛

# Who's My Neighbour?

Hey everyone! I want you to imagine something with me. Ready?

You're at the playground. You're having the BEST time. And then you notice a kid sitting by the fence all alone. They've fallen off the monkey bars. Their knee is bleeding. They're crying. And here's the thing — you don't know them. They don't go to your school. You've never seen them before in your life.

What would you do?

Hold that thought. Because Jesus once told a story about exactly this kind of moment. And it's one of the best stories ever told.

## A Dangerous Road

One day, a man was walking along a road from Jerusalem to Jericho. Now, this wasn't a nice road. It was rocky and winding, with big cliffs on each side — perfect hiding spots for robbers. And that's exactly what happened.

Robbers jumped out. They grabbed the man. They took everything he had — his money, his coat, even his shoes. Then they beat him up and left him lying in the dirt, hurt so badly he couldn't even stand. He was just lying there, in the hot sun, all alone, hoping — *praying* — that someone would come along and help.

And someone did come along! A priest. Now, a priest was someone who worked in God's temple. If ANYONE was going to help, it would be him, right?

The priest saw the man lying there. He saw the blood. He heard the groaning.

And you know what he did?

He crossed to the other side of the road. And he kept walking.

Gone. Just like that.

Then ANOTHER man came along — a Levite. He was also someone who worked at the temple, someone who was supposed to know all about loving God.

He walked over. He actually got close enough to look at the hurt man.

And then? He crossed to the other side of the road too. And off he went.

Can you imagine how that poor man felt? Lying there, watching two people see him and just… walk away? That must have felt even worse than the bruises.

## The Surprise Hero

But then — footsteps. Someone else was coming.

This time it was a Samaritan.

Now here's something important. Back in those days, the people listening to Jesus would have been SHOCKED. Jewish people and Samaritan people did NOT get along. They didn't eat together. They didn't talk to each other. They thought of each other as enemies. So everyone listening probably thought, "Well, THIS guy definitely won't help."

But the Samaritan saw the man on the ground, and something happened inside his heart. The Bible says he felt *compassion*. That's a big word that means his heart hurt because someone else was hurting. He didn't think, "Is this person from my group? Is this person my friend? Does this person deserve my help?"

He just saw someone who needed him.

So he knelt down in the dirt. He carefully cleaned the man's wounds with oil and wine — that was like medicine back then. He tore up strips of cloth and bandaged every cut. He lifted the man — gently, carefully — onto his own donkey, which meant the Samaritan himself had to walk.

He brought the man to an inn, which is like a hotel. He stayed with him through the night, making sure he was okay. And the next morning, he gave the innkeeper money and said, "Take care of him. If it costs more, I'll pay you back when I return."

He didn't just help a little bit. He helped ALL the way.

## So… Who Was the Neighbour?

After Jesus told this story, he asked a simple question: "Which of these three men was a neighbour to the man who got hurt?"

And the answer was obvious, wasn't it? The one who helped. The one who showed kindness. Not the important people who walked on by, but the one everyone expected to keep walking — and didn't.

Then Jesus said three powerful words: **"Go and do likewise."**

That means: go and do the same thing.

Here's what I love about this story. The Samaritan didn't help because it was easy. It cost him time, money, and energy. He didn't help because the man was his friend — they were strangers, maybe even supposed to be enemies. He helped because he saw someone who needed kindness, and he chose to give it.

## Your Turn This Week

Remember that kid at the playground? You know what to do now, don't you?

This week, I want you to try one thing. Look for someone who needs kindness — someone who ISN'T already your friend. Maybe it's the kid who sits alone at lunch. Maybe it's someone who looks sad. Maybe it's someone everyone else ignores.

And be their Good Samaritan.

You don't need oil and wine and a donkey. You just need to stop, see them, and be kind.

Because THAT'S what it means to be a neighbour.

Now — go and do likewise.

Gone. Just like that.

Then ANOTHER man came along — a Levite, which was like a temple assistant, another person who was supposed to know all about loving God.

He walked over. He actually got close enough to look at the hurt man.

And be their Good Samaritan.

You don't need oil and wine and a donkey. You just need three things:

**Stop. See. Be kind.**

Have you ever walked past someone who needed help — maybe a kid sitting alone at lunch, or someone who dropped all their books in the hallway — and you just... kept walking? 

*Pause.*

Yeah. Me too. It's okay to admit it. We've all done it.

But today I want to tell you a story that Jesus told a long, long time ago. And it might change the way you think about those moments.

---

So one day, a really smart man came up to Jesus. This guy knew all the rules. He'd studied them his whole life. And he asked, "What do I have to do to live the best kind of life — the kind that lasts forever?"

Jesus said, "Well, what do the rules say?"

The man answered, "Love God with everything you've got. And love your neighbour the same way you love yourself."

"That's right!" Jesus said. "Do that, and you'll be just fine."

But the man wasn't done. He crossed his arms and asked another question — and this is the big one:

**"But who is my neighbour?"**

See, he wanted Jesus to say, "Oh, your neighbour is your best friend. Your family. People who look like you and talk like you and live on your street." That would be easy, right?

But Jesus didn't say that. Instead, he told a story.

---

"A man was walking down a long, dusty road from Jerusalem to Jericho," Jesus began.

Now, this road was dangerous. It twisted through rocky hills and deep shadows — the kind of place where robbers liked to hide. And sure enough, robbers jumped out. They grabbed the man. They took everything he had — his money, his coat, even his shoes. They beat him up and left him lying in the dirt, bleeding, barely able to move.

He was all alone.

Then — footsteps. Someone was coming! A priest was walking down that same road. Now, a priest was supposed to be one of the *good* guys. He worked in God's temple! Surely he would help.

But the priest looked at the man lying there... and crossed to the other side of the road. He just walked right past.

Can you believe that?

Then someone else came along — a Levite. That's another important religious person. Someone who should *definitely* know better. He walked over, took a closer look...

And kept going.

The man in the dirt must have felt so alone. So forgotten. Like nobody in the whole world cared about him.

But then — more footsteps.

This time, it was a Samaritan.

Now here's the thing you need to know. In those days, the Jewish people and the Samaritan people did NOT get along. They avoided each other. They didn't eat together, didn't talk to each other, didn't even walk through each other's towns. If anyone had a reason to keep walking, it was this guy.

But the Samaritan stopped.

He knelt down in the dust right next to the hurt man. He opened his bag and pulled out oil and wine — that's what they used for medicine back then — and carefully, gently cleaned every wound. He tore strips of cloth and wrapped the man's cuts. He lifted the man up onto his own donkey, which meant the Samaritan had to walk the rest of the way on his own tired feet.

He brought the man to an inn — kind of like a hotel — and took care of him all night long. And the next morning, he went to the innkeeper and pulled out his own money. "Look after him," the Samaritan said. "Whatever it costs, I'll pay you back."

Then he left. No selfie. No thank-you card. He just did it because it was right.

---

Jesus looked at the smart man and asked, "So — which of those three was a real neighbour to the man who got hurt?"

The answer was obvious, wasn't it?

"The one who was kind to him," the man said.

Jesus nodded. "Go and do the same."

---

Here's what I love about this story. The two "important" people walked past. But the one everybody expected to *not* care? He's the one who stopped.

That tells us something huge: **your neighbour is anyone who needs you right now.** Not just your best friend. Not just someone who's nice to you first. *Anyone.*

The new kid who doesn't know where to sit. The person everyone else ignores. The kid who's a little bit different from you.

*They* are your neighbour.

---

So here's my challenge for you this week. Just one thing.

Find someone who needs a little kindness — someone you might normally walk past — and **stop.** 

Say hello. Sit with them. Help them pick up their books. Share your snack. You don't have to do something huge. You just have to *not keep walking.*

That's it. That's what a Good Samaritan does.

And who knows? You might be the best part of someone's whole day.

Now go and do the same. 💛

## A Man on a Dangerous Road

One day, a man was walking along a rocky, dusty road from Jerusalem to a city called Jericho. It was a long road. A lonely road. The kind of road where you could hear your own footsteps echoing off the hills.

And then — *whoosh* — robbers jumped out from behind the rocks!

They grabbed the man. They took everything he had — his money, his coat, even his shoes. Then they beat him up and left him lying on the side of the road. He was hurt. Badly hurt. He couldn't get up. He couldn't walk. He could barely call for help.

He just lay there in the dirt, under the hot sun, hoping — *please* — that someone would come along.

And someone did.

## The First Person Walks By

A priest came walking down that same road. Now, a priest was someone who worked in God's temple. Someone who was supposed to know *all about* loving God and loving people.

The priest saw the man lying there. Bleeding. Hurting.

And you know what he did?

He crossed to the other side of the road. And kept walking.

Can you believe that? He just… walked away.

## The Second Person Walks By

Then another man came along — a Levite. He was another important religious person. Someone everyone respected.

He walked over. He actually *looked* at the hurt man. He saw the blood. He saw the bruises.

And then he did the same thing. He stepped to the other side of the road and walked right past.

Two people. Two people who should have known better. And neither one helped.

The hurt man must have felt so alone.

## Then Came the Surprise

Now, here's where the story gets really interesting.

A *Samaritan* came down the road.

And here's the thing you need to know: the people listening to Jesus tell this story did NOT like Samaritans. At all. Samaritans and Jewish people had been angry at each other for hundreds of years. They didn't eat together. They didn't talk to each other. They thought of each other as enemies.

So when Jesus said "a Samaritan came along," everyone listening probably thought, "Oh no. What's *he* going to do?"

And what did the Samaritan do?

He stopped.

He knelt down in the dirt right next to that hurt man. He didn't care that they were supposed to be enemies. He didn't care that it might be dangerous, or messy, or inconvenient.

He poured cool oil and wine on the man's wounds — gently, carefully — to clean them and stop the stinging. He tore strips of cloth and wrapped up every cut. Then he lifted the man up — *carefully, carefully* — and set him on his own donkey.

He walked beside him all the way to an inn. He put the man in a warm bed. He stayed with him through the night.

And the next morning, before he left, he took out his own money and gave it to the innkeeper. "Take care of him," the Samaritan said. "If it costs more, I'll pay you back when I return."

He gave his time. His money. His donkey ride. His whole evening and night. For a complete stranger. For someone who was supposed to be his *enemy*.

---

## So What Does This Mean for Us?

After Jesus told this story, he asked a simple question: "Which one was a real neighbour to the hurt man?"

And the answer was obvious, wasn't it? The one who *helped*.

Then Jesus said three words that changed everything:

**"Go and do likewise."**

Be the one who stops.

Be the one who doesn't walk past.

Be the Good Samaritan.

# The Good Samaritan: Be Kind to Everyone!

---

**Hands up if you've ever seen someone drop something and nobody helped them pick it up.**

Maybe it was in the playground. Maybe it was on the bus. Someone drops their bag, their books go everywhere — and people just walk past. Has that ever happened to you? How did it feel?

Today we're going to hear a story Jesus told about exactly that kind of moment. Except in this story, the stakes were a LOT higher than dropped books.

---

## The Story

A man was travelling along a road. It was hot. Dusty. Lonely. And then — *bang* — robbers jumped out from behind the rocks.

They grabbed his bag. They tore his coat. They hit him and left him lying in the dirt at the side of the road. He couldn't move. He couldn't call for help. He was just lying there, hoping someone — *anyone* — would come.

And someone did come! A religious leader came walking down that road. This was a really important, respectable man. Surely *he* would help?

The man on the ground must have thought, *"Yes! I'm saved!"*

But the religious leader looked over... and crossed to the other side of the road. He just kept walking.

*Ouch.*

Then another important man came along. Same thing. He took one look and walked on by.

Can you imagine? You're hurt. You're scared. And people just keep walking past like you're invisible.

But then — footsteps. Someone else was coming.

Now here's where the story gets interesting. The person who came was a Samaritan. And in those days, Jewish people and Samaritans didn't like each other. At *all.* They didn't talk to each other. They didn't help each other. If you'd asked the man lying in the road, "Would a Samaritan ever help you?" he probably would have said, "Absolutely not. No way."

But this Samaritan stopped.

He knelt down in the dirt next to the man. He cleaned his cuts — carefully, gently. He tore up cloth to make bandages. He lifted the man onto his own donkey and walked alongside him all the way to an inn.

Then he paid for the man to stay there and rest. He said to the innkeeper, *"Look after him. If it costs more than this, I'll pay you back when I return."*

He didn't have to do any of that. This man wasn't his friend. This man was from a group of people who probably didn't even *like* Samaritans. But none of that mattered.

He saw someone who needed help — and he helped.

---

## Why Does This Matter?

Jesus told this story because someone had asked him a question: *"Who is my neighbour?"* In other words — who do I actually have to be kind to? Just my friends? Just people who look like me?

And Jesus basically said: *everyone.*

Your neighbour isn't just the person next door. Your neighbour is the kid at school who nobody sits with at lunch. It's the new child who doesn't know anyone yet. It's someone who speaks a different language, or looks different, or comes from a different place.

Being kind is easy when it's your best friend. The *real* test of kindness is when it's someone you don't know — or someone you find difficult.

The Good Samaritan didn't stop and think, *"Hmm, do I like this person enough to help?"* He just saw a need and met it.

That's the kind of kindness Jesus is talking about. Not just kind feelings on the inside — but kind *actions* on the outside.

---

## Your Challenge This Week

Here it is — your one Good Samaritan challenge for this week:

**Find someone who needs a small act of kindness — and do it.**

Maybe someone's sitting alone. Go and sit with them. Say hi.

Maybe someone drops something. Pick it up.

Maybe someone looks sad. Ask if they're okay.

It doesn't have to be dramatic. You don't need a donkey. You just need to *notice* people — and then do something about it.

The Good Samaritan didn't walk past. He stopped.

**This week, be someone who stops.**

---

*"Go and do likewise."* — Jesus (Luke 10:37)

# The Good Samaritan: Be Kind to EVERYONE

---

**Hands up if you've ever seen someone looking sad or left out.**

*(pause)*

Maybe at lunch, someone was sitting all alone. Maybe someone dropped all their books and everyone just walked past. What did you do? What did you *want* to do?

Today we're going to hear a story that Jesus told — a story about someone who did something really surprising. And by the end, I think you're going to want to be just like him.

---

## A Very Dangerous Road

Picture this. A man is walking along a rocky, dusty road. The sun is blazing. There's nowhere to hide. And suddenly — *crash, bang, wallop* — robbers jump out from behind the rocks!

They grab everything he has. His bag. His money. His sandals. They push him to the ground and run away laughing.

The man is lying in the dirt. He's hurt. He's scared. He can't even get up.

Now, along comes the first person. A priest — like a very important religious leader. He sees the man lying there. He looks at him. And then... he crosses to the other side of the road and keeps walking.

*Hmm.*

Then comes another important man — a Levite, someone who worked in the temple. He walks up close, has a good look, and then... he crosses over too. And keeps walking.

Can you imagine? Two people just *leaving* him there?

The poor man must have thought, *"Is nobody going to help me?"*

---

## Here Comes the Surprise

Now. Here's the bit that would have made everyone listening to Jesus go quiet.

Along comes a Samaritan.

Does he say, "Well, he's not *my* kind of person"?

Your neighbour is *anyone who needs your help.*

The priest and the Levite — they probably thought they were good people. But when it really mattered, they looked away.

You can do that too.

**Go and do the same.**

---

*Now — who's going to be a Good Samaritan this week?*

Alright, everyone, gather round! I’ve got a question for you. What would you do if you saw someone who needed help? Let’s say you’re at the playground, and you see someone fall off the swing and skin their knee. They’re sitting there, and they look really sad. Would you go over and ask if they’re okay? Would you maybe even run and get a grown-up? I bet most of you would! Helping feels good, doesn’t it?

But… what if that person wasn’t someone you knew? What if they were someone you didn’t usually play with, or someone you thought was… different? Hmm. That can be a little trickier. Well, a long time ago, a man named Jesus told a story about exactly this. It’s called the story of the Good Samaritan, and it’s one of my favourites. Let’s pretend we’re there.

Once, there was a man walking down a long, dusty, winding road from Jerusalem to Jericho. The sun was hot, the rocks were sharp, and it was a road where sometimes not-so-nice people hid. And guess what? Some robbers did jump out! They grabbed the man, took his money and his bag, tore his clothes, and hit him hard. Then they ran away, leaving him lying hurt and all alone in the dirt. Ouch!

He couldn’t get up. He just lay there going, “Help… please, someone help me.”

Soon, he heard footsteps! *Crunch, crunch, crunch* on the gravel. It was a priest, a very important religious leader, walking down the same road. The hurt man must have thought, “Oh good, he’ll help me!” But the priest saw the hurt man, wrinkled his nose, and quickly walked way around him on the other side of the road. He didn’t stop. He just kept going.

A little later, more footsteps! This time it was a Levite, another important man who worked at the temple. He walked right over to the hurt man, stopped, and looked at him. The hurt man probably felt a little spark of hope. But then… the Levite shook his head, turned around, and walked away, too. No help.

The man in the dirt must have felt so sad and scared. Two people who *should* have helped just… didn’t.

Then, he heard the *clip-clop* of a donkey’s feet. Someone else was coming. Now, this person was a Samaritan. Here’s the thing: in that time, the hurt man (who was a Jew) and Samaritans did *not* get along at all. They were like two sports teams that are huge rivals, or two groups of kids who never, ever talk to each other. They were taught to ignore each other, to think the other group was bad.

So when the hurt man saw it was a Samaritan, he probably thought, “Oh no, he’ll be the meanest of all.”

But he was wrong.

The Samaritan saw the man, and his heart went *thump* with pity. He didn’t see a rival or a stranger. He just saw a person who was hurting. He rushed over! He knelt down in the dusty dirt. He gently cleaned the man’s cuts with oil and wine (which stung a bit, but helped!), and he wrapped them up with soft bandages, just like a doctor. He was so gentle.

Then, he did something amazing. He carefully lifted the hurt man onto his own donkey. *Clip-clop, clip-clop*, the Samaritan walked beside him, leading the donkey all the way to a little inn, which was like a hotel. He didn’t just drop him off. He stayed all night, making sure the man was comfortable.

The next morning, the Samaritan had to travel on. But he gave the innkeeper two whole silver coins – that was a lot of money! – and said, “Please take care of this man. And if you spend any more money looking after him, I’ll pay you back next time I come.” He promised! He made sure the hurt man would be okay long after he was gone.

So, let’s think. Who in the story was truly kind?

Not the important priest. Not the important Levite. It was the Samaritan, the one nobody expected to help! His kindness was a **surprise** kindness. He helped someone who was different, someone who might not even like him. He didn’t let those old, grumpy rules about “us” and “them” stop his heart from being good.

That’s the big, shining lesson Jesus wanted us to learn: **Kindness is for everyone.** Not just for your friends. Not just for people who look like you or talk like you. *Everyone.* A kind heart doesn’t see “different.” A kind heart just sees “person who needs a friend.”

So, how can you be a Good Samaritan this week? It doesn’t have to be as big as rescuing someone from robbers! Here’s one concrete thing to try:

**Look for someone who looks left out or lonely, and be the first to say hello.**

Maybe it’s the new kid in class who’s sitting alone at lunch. Maybe it’s someone in your neighborhood you don’t usually play with. Maybe it’s just someone who looks like they’re having a sad day. Walk over. Give them a smile. Ask, “Do you want to play?” or “Are you okay?”

That’s it! That’s your mission. Be the surprise kindness in someone’s day. Be the person who stops, helps, and cares—no matter what.

Because the world needs more Good Samaritans. And I know you can be one.

Hey there, amazing helpers! Let me ask you a question to start.

Have you ever seen someone who looked like they needed a hand? Maybe it was someone on the playground who fell down and skinned their knee. Or maybe it was the new kid at school who was sitting all alone at lunch. What did you do? Did you go over and help?

Today, I want to tell you a story that a very wise teacher named Jesus told a long time ago. It’s called the story of the Good Samaritan, and it’s all about what it really means to be a good helper. It might surprise you!

First, let’s picture the scene. Imagine a long, dusty, winding road, with big rocks and scrubby bushes all around. The sun is hot. A man is walking down this road, all by himself. Suddenly, some robbers jump out from behind the rocks! They knock him down, grab his bag, tear his clothes, and hurt him badly. Then they run away, leaving him lying in the dirt, all alone and hurting.

Ouch. That’s a really bad day, isn’t it?

After a little while, the hurt man hears footsteps coming down the road. *Crunch, crunch, crunch* in the dust. He thinks, “Oh, good! Someone is coming to help me!” The first person to come by was a very important religious leader. He saw the hurt man lying there… and then he walked way around him on the other side of the road! He didn’t stop. He just kept going.

Hmm. That’s not very helpful.

A little later, a second man comes down the road. This man was also someone who worked in the temple, a place of worship. He stopped and looked at the hurt man. But then… he also walked right on by! He didn’t stop either.

Double hmm. The hurt man must have felt so sad and scared.

Then, a third traveler comes along. Now, this man was a Samaritan. In Jesus’ time, the people listening to this story *did not like* Samaritans at all. They were taught that Samaritans were different, wrong, and not to be friends with. They would have been shocked that a Samaritan was even in the story!

But what did this Samaritan do?

When *he* saw the hurt man, his heart went, *"Oh, no! That poor man!"* He didn’t see a stranger or an enemy. He just saw a person who was hurting. He ran right over to him!

He knelt down in the dusty dirt. He was very gentle. He used his own water and a clean cloth to wash the man’s cuts and scrapes. He poured soothing oil and wine on them to help them feel better. Then, he wrapped up all the wounds with soft bandages. He was like a doctor right there on the side of the road!

But he didn’t stop there. He carefully lifted the hurt man onto his own donkey. He walked beside him, holding him steady, all the way to the nearest inn, which was like a small hotel. He took care of him all night.

The next morning, the Samaritan had to leave to continue his journey. But he paid the innkeeper some money and said, “Please take care of this man. If it costs more than this, I’ll come back and pay you when I return.” He made sure the hurt man would be okay even after he was gone.

Wow!

Jesus asked the people listening, “Which of these three was a good neighbor to the man who was hurt?”

The answer was easy: “The one who showed him kindness.”

And Jesus said, “You go and do the same.”

So, why was this story so surprising and important? The two people you’d *expect* to help… didn’t. The one person nobody expected to help… *did*. And he did it in the biggest, kindest, most generous way possible. He didn’t just say, “Feel better soon!” He *stopped*. He *got messy*. He *spent his time and his money*. He helped someone who was different from him, someone who might not even like him. That’s real kindness.

The lesson is this: **Kindness is for everyone.** Not just for our friends. Not just for people who look like us, or talk like us, or play the same games we do. Kindness is for the kid who is left out. Kindness is for someone who is having a hard time, even if we don’t know them well. A Good Samaritan is someone who sees a need and decides to *do* something about it.

So, what’s one thing you can do this week to be a “Good Samaritan”?

Here’s my challenge for you: **Look for one person who might need a friend, and be that friend.**

It could be:
*   Sitting with someone who is eating alone.
*   Asking someone who looks left out of a game to join you.
*   Helping a younger sibling or classmate who is struggling to tie their shoe or carry something.
*   Simply giving a smile and saying “Hi!” to someone who looks sad.

You don’t have to pour oil on scrapes or pay an innkeeper! You just have to use your superpower—your kind heart—and take one small action. You can be the one who stops. You can be the one who helps.

Go be amazing Good Samaritans! I can’t wait to hear about the kindness you spread.

Hello everyone! I'm so glad to see all your bright, smiling faces today!

I have a question for you. Imagine you're at the playground, swinging super high, and suddenly you see a friend trip and fall. *Ouch!* Their knee is scraped, and they look really sad. What would you do? (Pause for a moment, let them think or call out answers).

That’s right! Most of you would probably run over, ask if they’re okay, and maybe help them up, right? Because that’s what friends do! We help people we know and care about.

But what if it wasn't your friend? What if it was someone you don't really know, or maybe even someone you sometimes argue with? Would you still help?

Today, I want to tell you an amazing story that Jesus told a long, long time ago. It’s about being kind to *everyone*, even people we might not expect.

One day, a very smart man asked Jesus, "Who is my neighbor? Who should I be kind to?" It was a good question! So, Jesus told him this story:

Imagine a long, dusty road, winding through hills and valleys, from the big city of Jerusalem all the way to Jericho. It was a lonely road, and sometimes, not very safe.

One sunny morning, a man was walking all by himself on this road. He was just minding his own business, maybe humming a little tune, when suddenly – *WHOOSH!* – some mean robbers jumped out from behind a rock! They grabbed him, took all his money, even his nice coat, and then they hurt him badly, leaving him lying right there on the side of the road, all alone and in pain. Ouch!

After a while, who should come walking down the road? A very important church leader! He was wearing fancy clothes and probably had important things to do. He saw the man lying there, hurt. What do you think he did? Did he stop to help? No! He looked, he saw, and then he just walked right past him, on the other side of the road! Can you believe it?

Later, another person came along. This was a church helper, someone who worked in the temple. He also saw the hurt man. He even walked a little closer, took a peek, but then… he also walked right past him, without stopping! He just kept going!

Oh dear, this poor man was still lying there, all alone, hurting.

Then, someone else came down the road. Now, this person was a Samaritan. And here’s the thing: back then, Samaritans and Jewish people (like the man who was hurt) usually didn't get along at all. They often argued and didn't like each other. So, you might think the Samaritan would *definitely* walk right past, right?

But guess what? This Samaritan was different. When he saw the man, he didn't care that they were from different groups. He didn't care if they were "friends" or not. He just saw a person who was hurting.

And his heart felt so, so sad for the man. He didn't walk past. He *stopped*. He got right down beside him. He carefully cleaned the man's wounds and put special medicine on them to help them heal. Then, very gently, he lifted the man onto his *own* donkey! Can you imagine? He gave up his own ride to help someone he didn't even know!

He slowly led the donkey to a cozy little inn nearby. He took the hurt man inside, made sure he had a warm bed, and stayed with him, taking care of him all night long.

The next morning, when the Samaritan had to leave, he pulled out his money pouch. He gave two shiny silver coins to the innkeeper and said, "Please, take good care of this man. If it costs any more, don't worry, I'll pay you back when I return!"

Wow! What an amazing thing to do!

Now, back to Jesus and the smart man who asked, "Who is my neighbor?" Jesus asked him, "Which of these three people was a good neighbor to the man who was hurt?"

The smart man knew the answer. He said, "The one who showed him kindness."

And Jesus said, "Exactly! Now you go and do the same."

This story teaches us something super important. It tells us that our "neighbor" isn't just our best friend, or our family, or people who look exactly like us. Our neighbor is *everyone*! It's anyone we meet who might need a little kindness, a little help, or a little smile.

The Samaritan didn't ask, "Are you my friend?" or "Do I like you?" He just saw someone in need, and he chose to be kind. He chose to help. And that's what being a "Good Samaritan" means! It means having a big, kind heart that wants to help others, no matter who they are.

So, this week, I have a special mission for all of you. I want you to be a "Good Samaritan"! Look around you. Who might need a little help? Maybe someone in your class dropped their crayons and needs help picking them up. Maybe someone looks a little sad and could really use a friendly smile or a kind word. Maybe your brother or sister needs help tidying up their toys.

Your mission this week is to find *one* person – maybe someone who isn't your best friend, or someone you don't know very well – and show them kindness, just like the Good Samaritan. It could be a small thing, but it can make a really big difference!

Can you do that? Can you be a Good Samaritan this week? (Wait for enthusiastic responses). Awesome! I know you can! Let's all try to make the world a kinder place, one helpful act at a time!

He said: Imagine a man was walking all by himself on a long, hot, dusty road. This road was known for being a bit dangerous. Sadly, some mean robbers jumped out! **Title: The Surprise Hero on the Rocky Road**

**(Start by looking around the room with a big smile and high energy)**

Hi everyone! I am so happy to see you all today.

Before we start, I need everyone to use their imaginations. Can you do that? Great!

Imagine you are sitting in the school cafeteria or at the park having a snack. You are sitting with your absolute best friends. You’re laughing, telling jokes, and eating your favourite food.

Suddenly... *CRASH!*

A kid walking past your table trips over their own shoelaces. Their tray goes flying. Their apple rolls across the floor. Their milk splashes everywhere. It’s a huge, sticky mess.

Now, here is the tricky question. What if that kid isn’t your friend? What if that kid is someone who was mean to you yesterday? What if they root for the wrong sports team, or they always tease you?

Do you:
A) Laugh and say, "Ha! You deserved that!"
B) Pretend you didn't see it and keep eating?
C) Get up and help them clean the mess?

Hold that thought in your head! Don't say the answer yet.

Today, I want to tell you a story that Jesus told a long time ago. It’s a story about a man who had to answer a very similar question. It’s called the Parable of the Good Samaritan.

**(Lean in closer, lower voice to a storytelling whisper)**

The story starts on a road. But this wasn’t just any road. This was the road from Jerusalem to Jericho.

It was a scary road. It was steep, winding, and rocky. It went through deep, dark canyons where the sun barely shined. People called it the "Way of Blood" because bad guys—robbers!—liked to hide behind the big rocks and jump out at travelers.

One day, a Jewish man was walking down this lonely, dusty road. *Crunch, crunch, crunch* went his sandals. He was probably looking over his shoulder, feeling nervous.

Suddenly—*BAM!*

Robbers jumped out from behind a boulder! They weren't nice at all. They took the man’s money. They took his clothes. They beat him up and left him lying in the dirt, hurt and unable to move.

The poor man lay there under the hot sun. He was thirsty. He was bleeding. He needed help, fast.

**(Perk up)**
But wait! He heard footsteps. *Clip-clop, clip-clop.*

Someone was coming! It was a Priest. A Priest was a very important leader in the church. He knew all the rules about God. Surely, he would help!

The Priest saw the hurt man. He stopped. He looked. And then... he crossed to the other side of the road. He pulled his fancy robes tight so they wouldn't get dirty, and he walked right past. *Zoom.* He was gone.

Oh no!

A little while later, more footsteps. *Thump, thump, thump.*

It was a Levite. A Levite was like a helper in the temple. He sang songs to God and helped with the prayers. Surely *he* would stop!

The Levite saw the man. He slowed down. He looked at the mess. He probably thought, "Oh, that looks dangerous. What if the robbers are still here? I better hurry home."

So, he crossed the street and speed-walked away. *Whoosh.* He was gone too.

The hurt man was running out of hope. The sun was getting hotter. The flies were buzzing.

Then, he heard a donkey. *Hee-haw!*

Coming down the road was a Samaritan.

Now, pause! This is the most important part. Back in those days, the Jewish people (like the hurt man) and the Samaritans... they did *not* get along. They were enemies. They wouldn't talk to each other. They wouldn't share water. They wouldn't even look at each other. They were like cats and dogs!

If the hurt man had been awake, he probably would have thought, "Oh great. A Samaritan. He might kick me while I'm down."

Jesus told a story about this exact thing. But instead of a school hallway, it happened on a dusty, dangerous road.

**The Story: The Winding Road**

Picture a road that goes through the wild, rocky hills. It was the road from Jerusalem to Jericho. It wasn’t a nice, paved street like we have. It was hot, dusty, and full of sharp turns. And behind big rocks, bad guys liked to hide, waiting to steal things.

One day, a man was walking down this lonely road. Suddenly—*BAM!*

Robbers jumped out! They took his money, they took his clothes, and they beat him up. They left him lying in the dirt, hurt and unable to move. The poor man lay there under the hot sun, hoping someone would come to help.

He heard footsteps. *Crunch, crunch, crunch.*

He opened one eye. It was a Priest! A religious leader! This was a man who worked at the Temple. Surely, a man who loved God would help him?

The Priest saw the hurt man. He stopped. He looked at the mess. And then... he crossed over to the other side of the road. He walked right past, walking faster and faster until he was gone.

The hurt man groaned. But then, he heard more footsteps. *Pat, pat, pat.*

It was a Levite! Levites were the Priest’s helpers. They knew all the rules about being good. The man thought, "Okay, the first guy missed me, but this guy will help."

The Levite looked at the man. He might have thought, "Ew, too much blood," or "I don't want to be late for dinner." And just like the first man, he crossed the street and walked right past.

Now the man was really scared. He was alone. The sun was going down.

Then, he heard the *clip-clop, clip-clop* of a donkey.

**The Surprise Hero**

Coming down the road was a Samaritan.

They didn't talk to each other. They didn't share food. They didn't even live in the same towns. They really, really didn't like each other.

But the Samaritan didn't walk past.

When he saw the man, he didn't see an enemy. He saw a person who was hurting. And his heart felt sad for him.

The Samaritan stopped his donkey. He jumped off. He got down in the dirt. He used his own water and oil to clean the man’s cuts. He took his own clothes or bandages and wrapped up the wounds gently.

He didn't stop there. He picked the man up—and he must have been heavy!—and put him on his own donkey. That meant the Samaritan had to walk.

He took the man to an Inn (like a hotel), tucked him into a bed, and took care of him all night. The next morning, he paid the innkeeper with his own money—two silver coins—and said, "Take care of him. If it costs more, I’ll pay you back when I return."

Wow.

The man who was supposed to be the "bad guy" turned out to be the hero.

Jesus told this story because someone asked him, "Who is my neighbour?" The man thought "neighbour" just meant his friends, or the people who lived next door who looked like him and talked like him.

But Jesus was teaching us something huge.

Being a "Good Samaritan" doesn't mean just being nice to your best friends. It’s easy to share a cookie with your best friend. It’s easy to help your mom when she asks nicely.

Real kindness is helping someone even when they are different from you.
Real kindness is helping someone even if they haven't been nice to you.
Real kindness is stopping to help when everyone else just walks by.

The Priest and the Levite saw a problem to avoid. The Samaritan saw a person to love.

**The Challenge: Secret Agents of Kindness**

So, I have a mission for you this week. I want you to be a **Secret Agent of Kindness.**

This week, I don't want you to just be nice to your friends. I want you to look around. Look for the person sitting alone at lunch. Look for the person who dropped their pencil case. Look for the brother or sister who is annoying you.

When you see them, I want you to ask yourself: "What would the Good Samaritan do?"

Then, do one brave, kind thing. Help them up. Say hello. Share your toy.

Go out there and be the surprise hero in someone's day!

Have a great week, everyone!

The poor man lay there under the hot sun. He was thirsty, he was bleeding, and he was all alone. He needed a hero, fast.

**The Passerby Parade**

Luckily, he heard footsteps. *Clip-clop, clip-clop.*

The man probably thought, "Oh, thank goodness! Someone is coming!"

It was a Priest! Now, a Priest was a very important leader in God’s temple. He led the prayers and taught the people about God. Surely, a man who works for God will help, right?

The Priest saw the hurt man. He stopped. He looked.

But the Priest had a problem. He was worried about his rules. He thought, "If that man is dead, and I touch him, I will become 'unclean.' I won't be allowed to go into the temple or lead the prayers."

So, he made a choice. He chose his rules over helping a person. He crossed to the other side of the road and walked right past.

A little while later, more footsteps. *Shuffle, shuffle, shuffle.*

It was a Levite! A Levite was the Priest's assistant. He worked in the temple too, and he knew all the rules about being good and holy. The hurt man probably tried to lift his head, thinking, "Please, please help me."

The Levite looked at the man. He saw the blood. He saw the dirt. But he thought, "I have important places to be. I can't stop here. It’s too dangerous!"

And... he walked right past, too.

**The Surprise Hero**

Finally, a third man came riding on a donkey. *Hee-haw, hee-haw!*

But this man was a **Samaritan**.

Now, remember the Super Tigers and the Blue Sharks? That is exactly what Jews and Samaritans were like. They were enemies. They didn't talk. They didn't share food. They didn't like each other at all. They had hated each other for hundreds of years.

If the Priest and the Temple Assistant didn't stop, surely the Enemy would just laugh, right?

But the Samaritan didn't laugh. When he saw the Jewish man bleeding in the dirt, he didn't see a "Super Tiger" or an enemy. He saw a person who was hurting. And his heart broke for him.

The Samaritan did something brave. He stopped his donkey—even though it was dangerous to stop where robbers might still be hiding.

He jumped off. He didn't care about getting his clothes dirty or breaking religious rules. He knelt down in the dust. He used his own expensive oil and wine to clean the man’s cuts—which stings a little, but it helps heal!—and then he wrapped them up gently with his own bandages.

Then, he did something incredibly strong. He lifted the man up, put him on his own donkey, and walked beside them all the way to an inn—which is like a hotel.

The Samaritan didn't just drop him off, either. He stayed up all night taking care of him. And in the morning, he took out two silver coins—that was a lot of money back then!—and gave them to the hotel manager. He said, "Look after him. If it costs more, I’ll pay you back when I return."

He promised to come back. He gave his time, his money, and his safety to save his enemy.

**The Big Lesson**

Jesus finished the story and looked at the crowd. He asked, "Which of these three men was a neighbor to the man who got hurt?"

Was it the important Priest with the fancy robes? No.
Was it the busy Temple Assistant? No.
It was the Samaritan—the one who showed mercy. The one who showed love.

You see, kindness isn't about wearing the right clothes, going to the right building, or knowing all the rules. And kindness isn't just for your best friends or the kids on your team.

**Real kindness is helping anyone who needs help, even if they are different from you.**

The Samaritan got his hands dirty. He spent his own money. He helped someone who might not even say "thank you." That is what real love looks like. It’s not just a squishy feeling in your heart; it’s doing something with your hands and feet.

**Your Mission This Week**

So, I have a secret mission for you this week. I want you to be a "Good Samaritan."

I want you to keep your eyes open for someone who needs help, but—here is the trick—it has to be someone you don't usually play with. Not your best friend.

Maybe it’s:
*   Someone sitting all alone at lunch while everyone else is talking.
*   Someone who dropped their pencil case and pencils went rolling everywhere.
*   Someone who looks sad on the playground because they weren't picked for a game.

You don't have to have a donkey or bandages or silver coins. You just need a smile and a helping hand. You can go sit with them. You can help pick up the pencils. You can say, "Do you want to play with me?"

Let’s pray.

But wait… it’s *that* kid. The one who never shares the swings. The one who called your drawing "weird" yesterday. 

What would you do? Would you run over and help them pick up their crackers? Or would you pretend you didn't see anything and walk away? 

It’s really easy to be kind to our best friends, isn't it? If your best friend drops their lunch, you are helping them in three seconds flat! But being kind to someone we don't know very well, or someone who isn't always nice to us? That is super hard.

A long time ago, a man asked Jesus a question just like this. He asked, "Jesus, who exactly am I supposed to be kind to? Who is my neighbor?" 

Jesus didn't just give him a boring answer. He told him a story. Let's imagine it together. 

Close your eyes for a second. Picture a winding, bumpy dirt road. It goes through steep, rocky mountains. It’s hot, dusty, and a little bit spooky. This was the road to a city called Jericho. 

A Jewish man was walking down this road all by himself. Suddenly—*jump!*—a group of bad guys leaped out from behind the big rocks! They took the man's money, they took his clothes, and they beat him up until he was covered in bruises. Then, they ran away, leaving him hurt and alone in the dust. The poor man couldn't stand up. He could only wait and hope. 

*Crunch, crunch, crunch.* Footsteps! Someone was coming. It was a priest—a very important church leader. The hurt man probably thought, "Oh, good! A holy man! He will definitely help me." But the priest saw the hurt man, stopped, and then… walked all the way over to the *other* side of the road. He pretended he didn't even see him! 

A little while later, *crunch, crunch, crunch.* Another man came by. He was a temple helper. He walked right up, looked at the hurt man, and… nope. He crossed the road and hurried away, too. Now the hurt man was really sad. 

Then came a third man. He was riding a donkey. *Clip, clop, clip, clop.* This man was a Samaritan. 

Now, here is the really important part: Samaritans and Jewish people did *not* get along. In fact, they treated each other like enemies. They wouldn't even share a drink of water together. The hurt man probably thought, "Oh no, a Samaritan. He definitely won't help me." 

But the Samaritan didn't cross the road. He jumped right off his donkey. He ran over to the Jewish man. He didn't see an enemy; he just saw someone who was hurting. The Samaritan gently cleaned the man's cuts. He wrapped them up in soft bandages. Then, he lifted the heavy, hurt man onto his own donkey. He walked all the way to a cozy inn—like a hotel—and paid the owner his own money to take care of the man until he was all better. 

When Jesus finished the story, He looked at the man who had asked the question. "Which of those three men was a real neighbor to the hurt man?" Jesus asked. 

The man answered, "The one who showed him mercy. The one who helped." 

Jesus smiled and said, "Go and do the same." 

You see, Jesus was teaching us something amazing. A "neighbor" isn't just the person who lives next door to your house. And a neighbor isn't just your best friend. A neighbor is *anyone* who needs help. Jesus wants us to show kindness to everyone. Even people who are different from us. Even the kid who doesn't share the swings! 

Being a Good Samaritan means keeping our eyes wide open for people who need a little bit of love. So, here is your special mission for this week. I want you to do one simple thing to be a Good Samaritan. Look around your classroom or the cafeteria. Find someone who is sitting all by themselves, or someone who is struggling to carry something heavy. Walk right up to them, give them a big smile, and say, "Can I help you with that?" or "Do you want to sit with me?" 

You don't need a donkey or bandages to be a Good Samaritan. You just need a kind heart. Let's go out there this week and show everyone what true kindness looks like!

## The Superpower of Helping: Being a Good Samaritan

**(Target Audience: Ages 5-10)**

Hello, everyone! Are you ready for an amazing story? Good!

I want you to use your imagination for a minute.

**The Hook: What Would You Do?**

Imagine you are walking down the hall at school, and you see a kid—maybe someone you don't really know, or maybe even someone who sometimes bugs you—and they trip!

*CRASH!* Their backpack flies open. All their books, pencils, and maybe even their favorite snack scatter all over the floor. They look embarrassed, and maybe they’ve scraped their knee.

You are rushing to get to recess. What do you do?

Do you pretend you didn't see anything and walk quickly past? Or do you stop, even if it makes you a little late, and help them pick up their things?

Today, we are going to talk about a true superhero of kindness. Jesus told this story a long, long time ago to show us what it really means to be a good neighbor.

**The Dangerous Road**

Jesus told the people about a long, rocky, dangerous road that went from the city of Jerusalem down to another city called Jericho. It was a place where robbers liked to hide.

One day, a traveler was walking along this road all by himself. Suddenly, bam! Robbers jumped out! They grabbed his money, stole his clothes, and hurt him terribly. They left him on the side of the road, bruised, bleeding, and almost dead.

He couldn't move. He just lay there, waiting for someone to help.

The first person who came along was a very important man: a **Priest**. Priests had very serious, holy jobs. He saw the injured man. He saw the blood. But what did he do?

Did he stop? No. He walked right across the road, keeping as far away from the hurt man as possible. Maybe he was thinking, "I’m too busy! I’ll get my nice clothes dirty! Someone else will help him." And he hurried away.

The second person to come by was another important man called a **Levite**. He also worked in the temple, helping people learn about God. He stopped. He looked closely at the injured man. He probably sighed. And then, guess what? He also walked right around him and kept going. He didn't want to get involved.

**The Surprising Helper**

Now, the next person to come along was completely different. He was a **Samaritan**.

Now, this is where the story gets really surprising! In Jesus’ time, the Jewish people (like the injured man) and the Samaritans did *not* like each other. They were like two teams that were always arguing. They wouldn't share toys, they wouldn't eat together, and they certainly wouldn't help each other. They were supposed to be enemies.

But the Samaritan saw the injured man—a man who was supposed to be his enemy—lying in the dirt. And the Samaritan didn't think about rules, or how busy he was, or whose fault it was. He just saw someone who needed help.

He stopped immediately. He knelt down beside the man. He cleaned the man’s cuts with oil and wine, gently wrapped the man's wounds with bandages, and lifted him gently onto his own donkey.

Imagine how much that hurt man needed that help!

The Samaritan didn't just give him a quick wave and leave. He walked slowly, leading the donkey, until they reached a safe place—an inn, which is like a small hotel. He spent the night taking care of the man.

The next morning, the Samaritan had to leave. But before he went, he gave the innkeeper two silver coins. That was enough money to pay for the injured man’s room and food for a long time.

He told the innkeeper, "Please take care of him. If the bill is more than this, I will pay you the rest when I come back."

**The Big Lesson: Who Is Your Neighbor?**

Jesus asked everyone listening, "Which of those three men acted like a true neighbor to the man who was robbed?"

The answer was clear: the Samaritan!

The Priest and the Levite had good reasons to be busy, but they failed the test of kindness. The Samaritan showed that being a good neighbor isn’t about being friends with someone, or liking how they look, or even if they are on your side.

**A good neighbor is anyone who needs your help, right now!**

When Jesus told us to be like the Good Samaritan, he was giving us a superpower. The superpower of looking past differences and choosing kindness first. It means being brave enough to stop and help, even if it feels inconvenient or awkward.

**Your Mission This Week**

We can all be Good Samaritans this week! But how?

It doesn’t have to be a big, dramatic rescue on a dangerous road. It can be small acts of amazing kindness.

Here is your concrete mission for this week:

**Look for someone who looks lonely or left out—maybe someone sitting by themselves at lunch or recess. Go up to them and ask them to play, or ask them if they want to share your crayons, or just say hello.**

When you choose to notice someone who is struggling, and you choose to help them, you are being a Good Samaritan. You are showing the world the superpower of kindness! Let’s go out and be heroes!

Hi everyone! I am so excited to talk to you today about one of the most powerful superpowers we all have. It’s not flying, and it’s not super-strength, but it’s something called **kindness**!

### The Hook: What Would You Do?

Raise your hand if you’ve ever been playing outside and maybe tripped over a root or scraped your knee. Ouch, right?

Now, imagine this: You are walking through the hallway at school. You see a kid you don't know very well, maybe someone from a different grade, and they trip right in front of the water fountain. They fall down hard, and all their papers and crayons go flying everywhere. They look embarrassed and maybe a little hurt.

You have a choice. Do you keep walking because you don't know their name, and you don't want to be late for class? Or do you stop, even if it takes a minute, and help pick up their things?

That choice—to stop and help—is exactly what a very smart man asked Jesus a long, long time ago. He asked, **"Who is my neighbor? Who do I have to be kind to?"**

Jesus didn't just give a simple answer. He told a story—a famous story—that changed how people thought about kindness forever.

### The Story of the Dusty Road

Jesus told the crowd about a man who was walking alone on a long, dangerous, dusty road. It was a road where robbers liked to hide.

Sadly, the man was attacked! The robbers stole his clothes, took his money, hurt him badly, and left him lying by the side of the road, half-dead and totally helpless.

Soon, someone came walking down that road. This was a very important person—a Priest. He worked in the temple, and his job was to help people and teach them about God.

The Priest saw the injured man. Did he stop? No. He looked at the poor man, maybe shook his head, and then he crossed the street to the other side and kept walking. He decided it was too messy, or maybe he was too busy.

A little while later, another important person came along. This was a Levite. He also worked in the temple and knew all the rules about being good.

The Levite stopped. He looked closely at the injured man. He might have thought, "Wow, that looks bad." But then he thought, "I don't know this guy. It's not my problem." And guess what? He crossed the street, too, and walked right past.

### The Big Surprise

Now, here comes the third traveler. This was a man from a place called Samaria.

This is the part of the story that would have made the people listening to Jesus gasp!

Why? Because in Jesus's time, people from Samaria and the local people were like rival teams who had a big, long-lasting argument. They didn't like each other, they didn't talk to each other, and they certainly didn't help each other. If you were hurt, a Samaritan was the *last* person you’d expect to stop.

But this Samaritan was different. When he saw the man lying there, his heart broke. He didn't care that the man was a stranger, or that they were from different places. He only cared that the man was hurt and needed help.

The Samaritan knelt down right there in the dust. He cleaned the man’s wounds very gently and wrapped them up with clean cloth. He poured oil and wine on the cuts to help them heal.

He carefully lifted the injured man onto his own donkey—meaning the Samaritan now had to walk!—and he brought him to a safe place called an inn, which is like a small hotel.

He stayed there all night, taking care of the man. The next morning, when the Samaritan had to leave, he paid the innkeeper money. He said, "Please take care of him. Make sure he has everything he needs. If it costs more, I will pay you back when I return."

He didn't just help a little bit; he helped completely.

### The Lesson: Kindness for Everyone

When Jesus finished the story, he asked the person who asked the question, "Which of these three people was a neighbor to the man who was attacked?"

The answer was clear! It was the Samaritan—the one who showed kindness and mercy.

Jesus showed us that our neighbor isn't just your best friend, or your cousin, or the kid who sits next to you in class. **Our neighbor is anyone who needs our help.**

Kindness means helping even the people we don't know. It means helping the people who look different from us. It means being brave enough to stop when everyone else is walking by.

The Priest and the Levite were worried about their schedules and their rules. The Samaritan was worried about the *person*.

Jesus told everyone: **"Go and do the same."** Be a Good Samaritan!

### Your Mission This Week

You can be a superhero of kindness every single day. Here is your mission for this week:

Look around at recess, or in the lunchroom, or maybe on the bus. Is there someone sitting by themselves? Someone who looks lonely or maybe a little sad?

Your job is to be like the Good Samaritan. You don’t have to bandage a scraped knee, but you can use your words to heal loneliness.

Go over, say hello, and ask them to play, or ask if they want to sit with you. That is a giant, powerful act of kindness.

Remember: Kindness is the superpower that helps everyone feel loved and safe. Let’s all go out there and be Good Samaritans this week! Thank you!

You have a choice. Do you keep walking because you don't know their name, and you don't want to be late for class? Or do you stop, even if it takes a minute, and help pick up their things?

That choice—to stop and help—is exactly what a very smart man asked Jesus a long, long time ago. He asked, **"Who is my neighbor? Who do I have to be kind to?"**

Jesus didn't just give a simple answer. He told a story—a famous story—that changed how people thought about kindness forever.

Jesus told this story to answer that question. Close your eyes and imagine you're there. Feel the hot sun. Hear the donkey’s hooves clip-clopping on the stones as the story begins.

### The Story of the Dusty Road

Jesus told the crowd about a man who was walking alone on a long, dangerous, dusty road. It was a road where mean robbers liked to hide.

Sadly, the man was stopped by mean robbers! They stole his clothes, took his money, hurt him, and left him lying by the side of the road, too hurt to stand up or call for help.

Soon, someone came walking down that road. This was a very important person—a Priest. He worked in the temple, and his job was to help people and teach them about God.

The Priest saw the injured man. Did he stop? No. He looked at the poor man, maybe shook his head, and then he crossed the street to the other side and kept walking. He decided it was too messy, or maybe he was **too busy.**

A little while later, another important person came along. This was a Levite—that’s like a special temple helper who knew all the rules about being good.

The Levite stopped. He looked closely at the injured man. But then he thought, "I don't know this guy. It's not my problem." And guess what? He crossed the street, too. He was **too busy too!**

### The Big Surprise

Now, here comes the third traveler. This was a man from a place called Samaria.

The crowd listening to Jesus leaned in. Who would it be? Surely not... a Samaritan? The crowd gasped! Some kids probably covered their mouths with their hands!

Why? Because in Jesus's time, people from Samaria and the local people were like rival teams who had a big, long-lasting argument. They didn't like each other, and they certainly didn't help each other. If you were hurt, a Samaritan was the *last* person you’d expect to stop.

But this Samaritan was different. When he saw the man lying there, his heart broke. He didn't care that they were strangers. He didn't care that they came from different places. He only cared that the man was hurt and needed help.

The Samaritan knelt down right there in the dust. He tore strips from his own clean shirt—*rip! rip!*—and tied them gently around the cuts. He poured oil and wine on the cuts to help them heal. (Back then, oil and wine were like their medicine—it helped keep the wounds clean.)

He carefully lifted the injured man onto his own donkey—meaning the Samaritan now had to walk!—and he brought him to a safe place called an inn, which is like a small hotel.

He stayed there all night, taking care of the man. The next morning, when the Samaritan had to leave, he paid the innkeeper money. He said, "Please take care of him. Make sure he has everything he needs. If it costs more, I will pay you back when I return."

He didn't just help a little bit; he helped completely, even though it cost him time and money.

### The Lesson: Kindness for Everyone

When Jesus finished the story, he asked the person who asked the question, "Which of these three people was a neighbor to the man who was attacked?"

The answer was clear! It was the Samaritan—the one who showed kindness and mercy.

Jesus showed us that our neighbor isn't just your best friend, or your cousin, or the kid who sits next to you in class. **Our neighbor is anyone who needs our help.**

The Priest and the Levite were worried about their schedules and their rules. The Samaritan was worried about the *person*. He was brave enough to stop when everyone else was walking by.

Jesus told everyone: **"Go and do the same."** Be a Good Samaritan!

### Your Mission This Week

You can be a superhero of kindness every single day. Here is your mission for this week:

Look around at recess, or in the lunchroom, or maybe on the bus. You are looking for a cue!

Look for someone sitting alone at a table. Is there someone who dropped their books and everything spilled out? Is there someone whose face looks sad or lonely? That is your cue to be a Good Samaritan.

You don’t have to bandage a scraped knee, but you can use your words and actions to heal loneliness.

Go over, say hello, and ask them to play, or ask if they want to sit with you. That is a giant, powerful act of kindness that makes the world a better place.

Remember: Kindness is the superpower that helps everyone feel loved and safe. Let’s all go out there and be Good Samaritans this week! Thank you!
