## The Superpower of Seeing Someone Who Needs Help

**(Start with a Hook)**

Hello, everyone! I have a super important question for you today. Imagine you are walking home from school, and you see a giant, juicy, bright red apple sitting right on the sidewalk. It looks delicious! You think, "Yummy, I’m going to pick that up!"

But then, right next to the apple, you see something else. You see your friend, Leo, who just tripped! He’s sitting on the ground, and his backpack has spilled open. His pencils are everywhere, and he looks a little bit sad.

What do you do first? Do you grab the apple and keep walking? Or do you stop and help Leo pick up his things?

*(Pause for a moment, let them think.)*

Most of you are probably thinking, "I’d help Leo!" That’s right! Helping someone who needs it feels good, doesn't it? Today, we are going to talk about why stopping to help, even when it’s hard or surprising, is one of the best things a person can do. It’s called **kindness**.

### The Story of the Road Trip

A long, long time ago, people told a story about a man who took a very long, dusty walk on a dangerous road. Let’s call him Mr. Traveler.

Mr. Traveler was walking when, suddenly, some mean people jumped out! They were not nice at all. They took everything he had and hurt him very badly. Then, they left him lying all alone on the side of the road. He was hurt, scared, and couldn't move.

Soon, two different people walked by.

The first person was a religious leader—someone everyone thought was very good and important. He looked at Mr. Traveler. He saw the cuts, the dirt, and the trouble. And what did he do? He walked right past him, on the other side of the road. *Swish!* He didn't stop.

The second person who walked by was another important person. He saw Mr. Traveler too. He shook his head sadly, maybe whispered, "Oh dear," and then he *also* kept walking. He didn't want to get involved.

It was getting dark. Mr. Traveler was still there, hurting and alone.

### The Surprise Helper

Then, someone unexpected came down that road. It was a man from a town called Samaria. Now, in those days, people from Samaria and the people Mr. Traveler came from did *not* like each other. They were like two sports teams that always argued!

When this Samaritan man saw Mr. Traveler lying there, he didn't care that they weren't friends. He didn't care that it might be messy or that he might get dirty.

He stopped!

This Samaritan didn't walk past. He ran *to* the man. He was kind!

He cleaned the cuts with some special oil and bandages. He lifted the hurt man onto his own donkey—imagine putting your own pet on the ground just to help someone else! He carried him slowly to a safe place, an inn, where he could rest.

And guess what? The Samaritan didn’t just drop him off. He stayed the night! He took care of the man until he felt better. The next morning, he even paid the innkeeper extra money and said, "If he needs anything else, please take care of him, and I will pay you when I come back."

Wow! That was incredible kindness!

### Why Was This So Important?

Think about the first two people. They were important, but they walked away. They thought, "That’s not my problem," or maybe they were too busy.

The Samaritan was the *least* likely person to stop. He was the person everyone expected to keep walking. But he chose to see someone who was hurting, no matter who they were or what group they belonged to.

Jesus, who told this story, wanted us to learn something very important: **Kindness has no limits.**

Kindness isn't just for your best friend, or your brother or sister, or someone who shares your toys. Kindness is for *everyone*. It’s for the new kid at school who looks lonely. It’s for the person who might have a different idea than you. It’s for the person who is having a bad day, even if you don't know them very well.

The Samaritan showed us that when we see someone who needs help—whether it’s a scraped knee, a dropped lunch, or just someone needing a smile—we should stop and be their helper. That is being a "Good Samaritan."

### Your Mission This Week

So, how can you use your superpower of kindness this week?

I want you to look for someone you don't usually talk to. Maybe it’s someone sitting alone on the playground, or maybe it’s a grown-up at the grocery store who looks stressed.

Your mission is this: **This week, find one person who looks like they need a little bit of help, and do one small thing to make their day better.**

It could be:
*   Holding the door open for someone.
*   Sharing a crayon when someone forgets theirs.
*   Asking the quiet kid at lunch, "What are you drawing?"

When you stop to help someone—even when you don't *have* to—you are being just like that amazing Samaritan. You are showing the world that your heart is big enough for everyone.

Go out there and be kind today! Thank you!

## The Day We Became Helpers

**(Start with a hook)**

Hello everyone! I have a question for you. Imagine you are walking home from school, and you see your favorite toy—maybe it’s a bright red truck or a sparkly unicorn—lying right in the middle of the sidewalk. It looks a little broken.

What do you do? Do you just walk past it because it’s not *your* toy? Or do you stop, pick it up gently, and try to fix it?

(Pause for a moment, let them think.)

Today, we’re going to talk about stopping. We’re going to talk about being a super-duper helper, even when it’s surprising!

Our story comes from a very old, very important book, and it’s about a man who showed us the very best way to be kind. It’s called the story of the Good Samaritan.

**(Retelling the Parable)**

A long, long time ago, there was a man traveling on a dusty, bumpy road. Imagine the sun beating down, making the road look like hot sand. This man was walking from one town to another.

Suddenly, some mean people jumped out! They took his money, they ripped his clothes, and they hurt him very badly. Then, they just left him there, lying on the hot, dusty ground. He was hurt, scared, and all alone.

Soon, two different people walked by.

The first person was a Priest. He saw the injured man. Did he stop? Nope. He quickly crossed to the other side of the road and hurried away. Maybe he was in a big rush, or maybe he felt a little scared.

Then, the second person came along. This was a Levite—someone who worked in the temple. He saw the poor man groaning on the ground. Did he help? No way! He also crossed the road and rushed past.

These two people saw someone in trouble, but they kept walking. They didn't want to get involved.

**(The Surprise Helper)**

But then, who came down that road? A Samaritan!

Now, here’s the secret: People back then didn't like Samaritans. They often argued about silly things, like which temple was the right one to visit. They were supposed to be enemies. A Samaritan seeing someone from the "other side" in trouble would usually just keep walking.

But this Samaritan saw the man. And guess what he did? He stopped!

He didn't look away. He didn't cross the road. He knelt right down beside the injured man. Can you imagine the smell of the dust and the worried look on the Samaritan’s face?

He didn’t care that the man was different. He didn’t care that they weren't friends. He just saw someone hurting.

The Samaritan gently cleaned the man’s cuts with oil and wine to make them feel better. He wrapped soft bandages all around the wounds. Then, he carefully lifted the man onto his own donkey! Think about that—he gave up his own ride!

He took the injured man to a safe place—an inn—and took care of him all night long. He made sure he was warm and safe. The next day, he paid the innkeeper extra money and said, "Please keep taking care of him. If it costs more, I will pay when I come back."

**(The Big Lesson)**

Wow! That Samaritan was amazing, right? He was the one people least expected to help, but he was the one who showed the biggest kindness.

What did the Samaritan teach us? He taught us that kindness isn't just for our friends or the people we like best.

Kindness is for *everyone*.

It doesn't matter if someone has different colored shoes than you, or if they eat different snacks, or if they are from a different class at school. If you see someone who needs help, you stop. If you see someone sad, you smile. If you see someone dropped their crayons, you pick them up!

Being a Good Samaritan means looking past the differences and seeing the person who needs your help right now. It means stopping when everyone else walks by.

**(The Concrete Challenge)**

So, how can you be a Good Samaritan this week? You don’t need a donkey or oil and wine!

Here is your mission: **This week, I want you to look for one person who seems lonely or left out.**

Maybe at recess, you see someone standing by themselves near the swings. Maybe in line, someone drops their lunch bag.

Your job is to go over, say hello, ask them to play, or help them pick up their things. You are stopping to help someone who might not expect it.

When you do that, you are shining a light just like the Good Samaritan did on that dusty road. You are showing the world that kindness is for everybody.

Are you ready to be a super-helper this week? I know you are! Thank you for listening!

**Imagine you are walking down the hallway at school.**

Suddenly, right in front of you, a boy trips and falls. *Wham!* His books go everywhere. His lunchbox pops open, and his apple rolls across the floor. Everyone stops and looks. Some kids giggle.

What do you do?

That is exactly the kind of question Jesus was asked a long time ago. A man asked, "Who is my neighbor?" He basically meant, "Who do I *have* to be nice to? Just my friends? Just people like me?"

To answer, Jesus told a story. It’s a story about a dangerous road and a surprising hero.

**The story starts with a man walking down a dusty, rocky road.** It was a lonely place, full of tall bushes and sharp rocks. Suddenly—BAM! Robbers jumped out! They didn’t just say "boo"; they beat the man up, took his money, and tore his nice clothes. Then, they ran away, leaving the man lying in the dirt, hurt and all alone.

A little while later, a Priest came walking down the road. This was a very important man, someone who worked in the temple. When he saw the hurt man, you think he would stop, right? But no. He saw the man, crossed to the other side of the road, and pretended he didn’t see him. He didn’t want to get involved.

Then, a Temple helper walked by. He saw the bleeding man, too. But he also crossed to the other side. He thought, "That looks like trouble. I don't want to get my clothes dirty." So, he kept walking.

Finally, a third man came down the road. He was a Samaritan. Now, this is the surprising part. Samaritans and Jews usually didn’t get along. They were like enemies. If this happened in a movie, you’d expect the Samaritan to ignore the guy, or maybe even kick him while he was down!

But look what the Samaritan did. When he saw the man, his heart went *thump-thump* with sadness. He didn't cross the street. He ran right over.

He cleaned the man’s cuts with his own water and wrapped them up with bandages. He lifted the man onto his donkey—kind of like giving him a ride on his own pony. He took him to a hotel and paid for a room! He even gave the hotel manager extra money and said, "Take care of him. If it costs more, I’ll pay you when I get back."

Jesus asked, "Which one was the real neighbor?"

A neighbor isn't just the person who lives next door. A neighbor is *anyone* who needs help. It could be the new kid at school who looks lonely. It could be someone who drops their gloves on the playground. It could even be someone who wasn't very nice to you yesterday.

Jesus showed us that kindness isn't about who *deserves* it. It’s about having a heart that sees a need and stops to help.

You don't have to be a grown-up to be a hero. You just have to be a Good Samaritan. Who will you help this week?

The road was very quiet. The man groaned, "Is anyone there?" But no one answered.

A little while later, a priest came down the road. This was a man who worked in the temple, someone everyone respected. He wore nice clothes and carried important books.

He saw the hurt man lying there. Surely he would stop, right?

But the priest looked at the dirt. He looked at the blood. He thought, "If I stop, I might get my clothes dirty. Or maybe the bad guys are still hiding."

So, the priest crossed to the other side of the road. He walked faster. He didn't look back.

Then, a temple helper walked by. He was also an important man. He saw the man, too.

He squinted his eyes. "That looks serious," he thought. "But I have a meeting to get to. I can't be late."

So, he also crossed to the other side and walked right on past. He kicked up dust as he hurried away.

Then came the surprise.

A Samaritan man came riding down the road on his donkey. *Clip-clop, clip-clop.*

Now, in those days, Jewish people and Samaritans were like enemies. Think of it like two rival sports teams that never play nice. They lived in different places and believed different things. If the hurt man had been awake, he might have been scared of the Samaritan!

But when the Samaritan saw the man, his heart hurt for him. He didn't see an enemy. He just saw someone who was hurt.

He didn't cross to the other side. He stopped. He pulled on the reins, and his donkey came to a halt. He got off and knelt right down in the dirt.

"Don't worry," the Samaritan said gently. "I can help you."

He poured cool oil and wine on the man’s cuts. It might have stung a little, but it cleaned the wounds. He wrapped them up with bandages. Then, he gently lifted the man onto his own donkey. The donkey carried them both to a safe place—an inn. An inn is like a hotel where travelers can sleep and eat when they are tired.

The next morning, the Samaritan had to leave, but he didn't want the man to be left with no money. He pulled out some silver coins.

"Take care of him," he told the innkeeper. "If it costs more to feed him and fix him up, I’ll pay you when I come back."

Jesus asked the people listening, "Which one was a neighbor to the man who was robbed?"

The answer wasn't the important religious guy. It wasn't the powerful guy. It was the enemy. The one who stopped.

The Samaritan was surprising because he didn't care if the man was different from him. He didn't care if it was inconvenient or messy. He just saw someone who needed help, and he did something about it.

That is the lesson for us today. **Be a neighbor to everyone.**

Being kind is easy when it’s your best friend. But a real neighbor—someone like the Good Samaritan—is kind to *everyone*, even people they don’t know very well or even people they might not get along with.

So, here is your challenge for this week. I want you to be a "Good Samaritan" on the playground.

Look for the kid who is sitting alone at recess, watching the others play. Or maybe someone who dropped their pencil box and is struggling to pick it up while other kids run past.

Help someone near, help someone far away. Be kind today and every day. **Be a neighbor to everyone!**

# The Surprise Helper: A Talk About Kindness

Hey everyone! I have a question for you.

Picture this: You're at recess, and you see someone trip and fall right in the mud. Their lunch goes flying—splash!—right into a puddle. Now they're messy AND hungry. But here's the thing... this kid isn't your friend. In fact, last week, they said something mean about your shoes. They're not very nice to you.

What would you do? Would you help them? Or would you think, "Not my problem" and walk away?

Hmm. That's a tricky one, isn't it? Let me tell you a story Jesus told about almost the exact same situation.

---

A long time ago, a man was walking on a winding, dusty road between two cities. The sun was blazing hot. Rocks scraped under his sandals. Suddenly—out of nowhere—robbers jumped out from behind the rocks! They grabbed the man, punched him, took all his money, and tore his clothes. Then they ran away, leaving him lying on the hard dirt road, hurt and barely able to move.

He just lay there, bleeding and scared, hoping someone would come.

And someone did.

A priest came walking down the road. A priest! That's like a pastor—someone who teaches people about God. The man on the ground must have thought, "Oh thank goodness! He'll help me!"

But the priest saw the hurt man... and crossed to the other side of the road. He looked away and kept walking.

Can you believe that?

A little later, another religious leader came by. A Levite—someone who worked in the temple! Surely HE would stop. But no. He saw the man, slowed down, and then crossed to the other side too. Kept walking.

The hurt man lay there alone. The hot sun beat down. His cuts stung. Maybe he thought no one would ever help.

But then—footsteps. Someone else was coming.

This man was a Samaritan. Now, here's something important: In those days, Samaritans and Jewish people did NOT get along. They argued about religion. They didn't talk to each other. Some people even walked the long way around just to avoid Samaritans. They were basically enemies.

So when the hurt man heard a Samaritan coming, he probably thought, "Oh no. He definitely won't help me. He might even make things worse!"

But you know what? The Samaritan saw the man, and his heart broke. He didn't see an enemy. He saw a person who was hurting.

He knelt down in the dirt. He poured soothing oil and wine on the man's cuts—ouch, then ahh, that feels better. He tore his own shirt to make bandages. Then he lifted the man onto his donkey—imagine how hard that was!—and walked alongside, holding him steady.

He took the man to an inn—a kind of hotel—and took care of him all night long. The next morning, the Samaritan took out his own money and gave it to the innkeeper. He said, "Take care of him. If it costs more, I'll pay you back when I return."

---

Wow. Did you hear that? He didn't just help a little. He gave his time, his donkey, his bandages, his money—and he promised to come back and pay more if needed!

Here's why Jesus told this story: Someone had asked him, "Who is my neighbor? Who do I need to be kind to?" And Jesus basically answered: The person who needs your help—that's your neighbor. Even if they're different from you. Even if you don't usually get along. Even if helping costs you something.

The priest and the Levite were "important" religious people. But they walked right past someone in need. The Samaritan was the last person anyone expected to stop. But he did. He showed what true kindness looks like.

---

So here's my question for you: Who might need your kindness this week?

Maybe there's a kid at school who sits alone at lunch. Maybe someone in your neighborhood who's different from you. Maybe someone who hasn't been very nice to you in the past.

Here's your challenge: This week, I want you to be a Good Samaritan. Find ONE person—especially someone you don't usually talk to—and do something kind for them. It could be as simple as sitting with them, sharing a snack, or saying, "Hey, want to play?"

That's it. One person. One act of kindness.

Because here's the thing Jesus wants us to understand: Kindness isn't just for our friends. It's for everyone. And when we help someone—anyone—who needs it, we're doing something beautiful.

So... who will your "neighbor" be this week?

# The Surprise Helper: A Talk About Kindness

---

Have you ever seen someone sitting alone at lunch and wondered, "Should I go sit with them?" Maybe they look sad, or maybe they're just new and don't know anyone yet. You want to help... but you're not sure. What if your friends think it's weird? What if you feel awkward?

Let me tell you a story Jesus told about someone who had to make that exact choice.

---

One day, a man was walking on a winding, rocky road between two cities. The sun was hot, and dust puffed up with every step. Suddenly—*CRASH!* Bandits jumped out from behind the rocks! They grabbed the man, took everything he had, and *whack, whack, whack*—they hurt him badly. Then they ran away, leaving him bruised and bleeding on the ground.

He couldn't stand up. He couldn't even crawl. He just lay there in the dirt, hoping someone would come.

And someone *did* come.

Footsteps echoed on the road. The hurt man squinted up. A priest! A religious leader from the temple! "Oh, thank God," the man thought. "He'll help me for sure."

But the priest saw the blood, made a face, and *hurried to the other side of the road*. He walked faster and faster until he disappeared around the bend.

The hurt man's hope crumbled.

A little later, more footsteps. A temple assistant this time. Surely *he* would stop! But no—the assistant peeked at the broken man, gulped, and crossed to the other side too. Gone.

The hurt man lay back down. Nobody was coming. Nobody cared.

Then—*clip-clop, clip-clop*. A donkey approached. On it sat a man from Samaria.

Now, here's something important: The hurt man was Jewish. And Jewish people and Samaritan people *did not like each other*. Not one bit. They argued about everything—where to worship, how to pray, who was right, who was wrong. Some Jewish people wouldn't even walk through Samaria; they'd take the long way around just to avoid Samaritans. They were enemies.

So when the hurt man heard a Samaritan coming, he probably thought, "Great. He'll laugh at me. Or make things worse."

But that's not what happened.

The Samaritan saw the man, and his heart squeezed. He didn't see an enemy. He saw a person who was hurting.

He climbed off his donkey and knelt in the dirt. He poured soothing oil on the man's cuts and bandaged his wounds. Then—hear this—he lifted the hurt man onto his *own* donkey and walked beside him, leading the animal slowly, carefully, all the way to a safe place called an inn.

When they arrived, the Samaritan took care of the man all night. The next morning, he dug into his money bag and gave coins to the innkeeper. "Take care of him," he said. "If it costs more, I'll pay you back when I return."

---

Do you see what happened? The people who *should* have helped—the priest, the temple assistant—walked right past. But the person everyone thought was an enemy? *He* was the one who stopped. *He* was the one who showed kindness.

Jesus told this story because someone asked him, "Who is my neighbor?" The person was hoping Jesus would say, "Your neighbors are the people who are like you—your friends, your family, people from your group."

But Jesus said, "Your neighbor is *anyone* who needs help. Even someone different from you. Even someone you might not like."

That's what kindness really means. It's not just being nice to your friends—that's easy! Anyone can do that. Real kindness is noticing when *anyone* needs help and choosing to do something about it.

---

So here's your mission for this week: Be a Good Samaritan.

Sometime in the next seven days, you'll see someone who needs help or encouragement. It might be a kid sitting alone at lunch. It might be someone who dropped their pencils. It might be a younger student who looks lost. It might even be someone who hasn't been very nice to you.

When that happens, I want you to remember the Samaritan on the donkey. Don't cross to the other side of the road. Cross *toward* them. Say something kind. Do something helpful.

And when you do, you'll discover something amazing: Kindness doesn't just help the other person. It changes *you* too.

---

**Let's pray:**

Dear God,

Thank You for loving us even when we were far from You.

Help us see the people around us who need kindness—especially the ones we might overlook.

Give us brave hearts to stop and help, not walk away.

Make us Good Samaritans this week.

In Jesus' name, amen.

What would you do if you saw someone fall on the playground and everyone else walked past? Would you stop? Or would you pretend you didn’t see?

Let me tell you a story.

One day a man was walking down a hot, rocky road. The sun baked the stones. Dust swirled. He had a bag, and he hummed a little tune. Suddenly, out of the tall bushes came some mean robbers. They shouted, “Give us your money!” They pushed him, took his things, and ran away. The man lay on the ground. His clothes were torn. He was bruised and bleeding. He groaned, “Ouch… help…” His voice was small on that big, quiet road.

First came a priest. He wore clean robes that smelled of perfume. He saw the man. He looked at him for a second. Then he hurried across the road. “Better not get dirty,” he said to himself. He kept walking.

Next came a Levite. He had a small bag of scrolls and a serious face. He also saw the man. He walked a little faster. He looked the other way, and walked on. Maybe he thought, “Someone else will help.” Maybe he was scared. Maybe he didn’t want trouble. But he did not stop.

Then came a Samaritan. He was not from the same town as the hurting man. People from his town and the man’s town didn’t usually like each other. They said mean things and stayed in different places. So everyone expected the Samaritan to keep going, too.

But guess what he did? He stopped.

He climbed down from his donkey. He knelt in the dust. He touched the hurt man’s arm and said, “Are you okay? Don’t worry. I’ll help you.” He used oil and wine he had — oil to soothe the sting and wine to clean the cuts. He tore his own cloth from his robe and wrapped the man’s wounds. He lifted him slowly onto the donkey. The donkey walked like a little rocking ship. The Samaritan held on until they reached an inn, a small house by the road.

At the inn he gave the owner two coins and said, “Look after him. If you need more, I’ll pay you back.” Then he got back on his donkey and rode away.

That story surprises us. Why? Because the priest and the Levite were the “religious” people. They knew a lot of rules about God and worship. People expected them to be helpers. The Samaritan was the person everyone usually ignored. He was an outsider. He was the one people would not trust. So when the Samaritan stopped — when he cleaned the wounds, shared his oil, gave money and stayed — it was a big surprise. It was a brave, kind surprise.

This story shows something important. Being kind is not only for friends. It is not only for people who look like you, talk like you, or live near you. Being kind is for everyone. The Samaritan didn’t say, “I’ll help if he’s my friend.” He saw someone in trouble and did what he could. He acted with love.

Kindness is more than feeling sad. Kindness is doing something. It is using your hands, your words, your time. It can be small. It can be big. It can be sharing your snack. It can be helping someone up. It can be sitting with a kid who looks lonely. It can be saying, “Do you want to play?” or “Are you okay?”

This week, try one thing to be a Good Samaritan. Find one person who looks left out at recess or lunchtime. Walk over and say, “Hi. Do you want to play with us?” If they say yes, great! If they say no, that’s okay — you tried. If someone is hurt or crying, tell a teacher and stay with them until help comes.

Remember three little steps:
- See someone who needs help.
- Stop what you’re doing and ask, “Are you okay?”
- Do something kind, even if it’s small.

You don’t need to be on a dusty road or give money. You just need to see, stop, and help. Be brave like the Samaritan. Be kind to everyone — even people who are different from you. That way, the world gets a little more gentle, one small act at a time.

Have you ever seen someone who needed help and wondered, What would I do?

Imagine this: you’re walking to school on a sunny day. The sidewalk is warm under your feet, and the air smells a little like popcorn because someone’s cart is popping corn nearby. Then you see a grown-up lying very still, with a scraped knee and a lot of dust on their face. What would you do?

Today I want to tell you a story about kindness, a story from a long, long time ago that Jesus told. It happened on a dusty road called the Jericho road. It’s a road that goes up and down hills, past stones and fields, the kind of road you could trip on if you’re not paying attention.

A traveler was walking along that road. He had a big bag and a heart full of plans. But suddenly, bad guys jumped out from behind a rock. They grabbed him, they beat him, they took his money, and they left him on the side of the road, hurt and hurting. The sun shone hot, and the traveler lay very still, not sure what would happen next.

First, a priest came by. A priest is someone who teaches about love and God. He saw the man, he looked away, and he kept walking. Then a Levite came along, another helper who knows about prayers and rules. He saw the hurt man too, but he hurried past in the opposite direction. “I must be careful,” you could almost hear him think. “I’m late. I’m busy. I don’t want trouble.” And he walked on.

Now, here’s the surprising part. On the same road, a third person came by. This person wasn’t from the same town as the hurt man. In fact, the man who stopped was a Samaritan. In those days, Jews and Samaritans didn’t trust each other. They were like rivals who forgot how to be kind. Some people would have said, “If the other group helps, that’s… surprising.” And it was surprising. But the Samaritan did something wonderfully ordinary and wonderfully brave: he helped.

“Are you okay?” the Samaritan asked softly. The man did not answer with words, just a groan of pain. The Samaritan opened his bag and found oil and wine—things people used to clean wounds and make them feel better. He poured the oil on the scrapes, then dabbed with the wine to cleanse them. It stung a little, but it felt better after a moment. He bandaged the cuts, wrapped them snugly, and kept talking in a calm, gentle voice, like a friend who never runs out of stories.

The Samaritan looked at the road and then at a hill, at the hurting man, and at his own horse. He did something that was brave in two ways. He placed the injured man on his own donkey, so the man could ride while the Samaritan walked. He led the horse along the rough path, one hand steady on the rein, the other keeping the man safe.

The road was hot, the dust rose, and the animals breathed hard. They came to a little inn by the side of a hill. The Samaritan spoke to the innkeeper in a plain, friendly way, saying, “Take care of him. If you need more money, I’ll pay you back when I pass this way again.” He watched the innkeeper lift the injured man onto a soft bed, and he stayed—along with the memory of the road’s quiet sighs—until the man could rest.

So why is this story so special? The first helpers—like the priest and the Levite—had important jobs. People expected them to stop and show kindness. But they didn’t. They chose safety or routine over mercy. The Samaritan, who was least expected to help, chose to love even when it cost him time and money.

From this, Jesus invites us to listen with our eyes and hearts. Kindness isn’t about agreeing with someone or sharing only with friends. It’s about seeing a person who needs help and choosing to help, even when it’s hard or when the other person is someone we don’t expect to be “our kind.” It’s about caring for the “neighbor” who is right in front of us—the person who needs a hand, a smile, or a moment of mercy.

So here’s the simple, memorable message: Be kind to everyone, not just your friends.

One concrete thing you can do this week to be a Good Samaritan: when you see someone who needs help, stop and help them. If you can, stay with them until they’re safe. Then tell a grown-up you trust what happened.

Imagine a man walking along a very long, bumpy road. The road goes from a hill near a big city to a small town away from the hills. It’s dusty, with pebbles that sparkle in the sunlight. The man’s clothes are worn, and his shoes are tight. He’s trying to get to help, but the sun is hot and the road is rough.

Along comes trouble. A big shadow—some robbers—jump out from behind a rock. They take what the man has and push him to the ground. The man groans. His heart beats fast. He can’t get up.

Soon, a man in a bright robe walks by. He is a priest. He stops for a moment, steps over the dirt, but then he sees the man and quickly turns away. He walks on the other side of the road, as if the hurt man is a shadow he doesn’t want to touch.

Not long after, another man comes along. He’s a Levite, a helper in the temple, dressed neat and careful. He glances at the hurt man, then looks away, and keeps walking. The road is quiet again, and the only sounds are birds and the man’s soft moans.

Then, out of nowhere, a traveler with a kind face comes down the same road. But this traveler isn’t from the same village as the one who was hurt. He’s a Samaritan, a person from a group many people didn’t trust. The Samaritan stops, looks at the man, and says, “Are you hurt? Can I help you?” His voice is warm, like cocoa by a morning fire.

“Please,” says the wounded man, “I need help.”

The Samaritan kneels and touches the man’s knee gently. He uses a little oil and wine he keeps in a small bag to clean the cuts. He sits the hurt man up a little and steadies him. “Don’t be afraid,” he says, and his voice is steady, safe.

He asks for a blanket, wraps the wounds, and even cleans the dirt from the man’s face. Then he lifts him up—carefully, slowly—and places him on his own donkey, so the man can ride while the road is bumpy. The man’s eyes are closed, but he smiles a tiny smile, glad for help.

They come to a bright inn, with a warm lamp in the window and the smell of bread and soup. The Samaritan speaks kindly to the innkeeper: “Take care of him. Here is money for today, and if there is more needed, I will pay you when I return.” The innkeeper nods, surprised and touched by this strange helper who doesn’t even belong to their town.

That night, the Samaritan stays awake, listening to the patient breathing, letting the lamp glow softly. He promises to return and finish paying for the care if more money is needed.

Jesus tells this story to teach a big idea: kindness isn’t about rules, who you know, or how you look. It’s about helping someone who needs help, even if that person isn’t your friend and even if people expect you to stay away. The man who helped was surprising. He came from a group that others often argued with or avoided. Yet he chose to help anyway. He didn’t wait for thanks. He didn’t choose to judge first. He chose to act with mercy.

So what’s the important rule here? Be a neighbor to anyone who needs help. A neighbor isn’t only the person you sit next to in class or your best friend. A neighbor is the person you see who is hurting or lonely or scared.

Now, a simple, ready-to-try idea for you.

This week, your one concrete thing to be a Good Samaritan: find one classmate who sits alone or who looks left out, and invite them to join your game or your lunch. Say, “Want to play?” or “Let’s sit together.” If you can, you can also offer a small help—carry something, hold a door, share a snack—anything that makes another person feel cared for.

You can be brave like the Samaritan. You can choose to help because helping is powerful, even if you’re not sure what will happen next. Kindness grows when we practice it, one small step at a time.

So, who will you invite to sit with you today? Who will you help this week? Let’s be neighbors—every day, in little and big ways. Because kindness, shared with many people, makes the world brighter, like that lamp in the inn window. And that is a good, true way to live.

DTnsZb16xOkuoQhz2NgU-.text:
What would you do?

Imagine you’re walking to school. You hear a thump. You turn the corner and see someone sitting on the ground. Their backpack is open. Books and pencils are everywhere. Their knee looks sore. They look like they might cry.

Do you keep walking because you’re in a hurry?  
Do you look away because you don’t know them?  
Or do you stop and help?

Jesus once told a story about a moment just like that—only bigger, scarier, and much more surprising.

A man was travelling down a long, dusty road. The sun was hot. The rocks were sharp under his sandals. The road was lonely. He was probably thinking, “Almost there. Just keep going.”

But then—suddenly—robbers jumped out!

“Give us your money!” they shouted.

They grabbed him. They took what he had. They shoved him to the ground. They hurt him. And then they ran away, leaving him there.

The man lay on the roadside. His clothes were torn. His face hurt. His heart pounded. He could barely move. He needed help. Badly.

After a while, he heard footsteps. Crunch, crunch, crunch on the gravel.

He lifted his head. “Someone’s coming,” he thought. “Thank you!”

It was a priest. A religious leader. A person people looked up to.

Surely he would help, right?

But the priest saw the hurt man… and then he did something shocking.

He crossed to the other side of the road.

He didn’t stop. He didn’t kneel down. He didn’t say, “Are you okay?” He just hurried away.

The hurt man probably watched him go, thinking, “Wait… what? Why?”

Soon, more footsteps. Crunch, crunch.

Another man came along. A Levite. He helped in the temple. He knew the laws. He knew the right prayers. He was supposed to be a “good” person.

He walked closer. He looked. Maybe he even frowned, like, “Oh no.”

And then… he crossed to the other side too.

He left.

Now the hurt man was still alone. Still hurting. Still scared. Maybe he thought, “Does anyone care?”

Then, more footsteps. Slow ones this time.

A Samaritan came walking down the road.

Now, here is the important part: Jewish people and Samaritans did not get along. They argued. They didn’t trust each other. Many of them wouldn’t even talk to each other. If you were picking someone to help a Jewish man, most people would not pick a Samaritan.

So the hurt man might have worried. “Oh no. Is he going to ignore me too? Or be mean?”

But Jesus says the Samaritan *saw* him—and felt compassion. That means his heart went, “Oh! That poor man!”

The Samaritan hurried over.

He didn’t say, “Is this my problem?”  
He didn’t say, “What if I’m late?”  
He didn’t say, “You’re not my friend.”

He knelt down in the dust right next to him.

“I’ve got you,” he might have said.

He cleaned the man’s wounds. He poured oil and wine on them—like medicine that stings a little, but helps. He wrapped him up carefully, like tying a bandage with gentle hands.

Then the Samaritan did something even harder. He lifted the hurt man onto his own animal. That means the Samaritan had to walk while the hurt man rode.

Step after step, down the road they went.

The Samaritan brought him to an inn—a place to rest. He stayed with him through the night. He made sure he had food and water. He checked on him.

And in the morning, the Samaritan gave the innkeeper money.

“Please take care of him,” he said. “If it costs more, I’ll pay you when I come back.”

Then Jesus asked the people listening a question: “Which person was a neighbour to the man who got hurt?”

It wasn’t the priest.  
It wasn’t the Levite.  
It was the Samaritan—the one who showed mercy. The one who acted with kindness.

That’s why this story is so surprising and important. The hero is not the person everyone expected. The hero is the person who *loved someone who was different*.

Jesus’ lesson is simple, but strong: kindness is not just for your best friends. Not just for people in your class. Not just for people who look like you, talk like you, or play the same games as you.

Kindness is for everyone.

So here’s one concrete thing you can do this week to be a “Good Samaritan”:

Pick one person you don’t usually play with—maybe someone new, someone shy, or someone who gets left out—and do one helpful thing for them. Sit with them at lunch. Invite them into your game. Help them pick up their things. Say, “Do you want to be my partner?” Use your words and your feet and your hands to show, “You matter.”

Because being a Good Samaritan starts with one brave choice:

Stop. Notice. Help.

“Give us your money!” they shouted.

They grabbed him. They took what he had. They shoved him down hard. They hurt him. And then they ran away, leaving him on the side of the road.

The man lay there. His clothes were torn. His face hurt. His heart pounded like a drum. He could barely move. He needed help. Badly. **And he was all alone.**

After a while, he heard footsteps. *Crunch, crunch, crunch* on the gravel.

He lifted his head just a little. “Someone’s coming,” he thought. “Thank you!”

It was a priest. A religious leader. A person people listened to and respected.

Surely he would help, right?

But the priest saw the hurt man… and then he did something shocking.

He crossed to the other side of the road.

He didn’t stop. He didn’t kneel down. He didn’t say, “Are you okay?” He just hurried away, like the hurt man wasn’t even there.

The man probably watched him go and thought, “Wait… what? Why?”

Soon, more footsteps. *Crunch, crunch.*

Another man came along. A Levite. That’s like a special helper in the church. He worked around the holy place. People thought he was a really good person.

He walked closer. He looked. Maybe he even made a worried face, like, “Oh no.”

And then… he crossed to the other side too.

He left.

Now the hurt man was still alone. Still hurting. Still scared. He might have thought, “Does anyone care about me at all?”

Then, more footsteps. Slower ones this time. *Thump… thump… thump…*

A Samaritan came walking down the road.

Now, here is the important part: Jewish people and Samaritans did not get along. They argued. They didn’t trust each other. Lots of them wouldn’t even talk to each other. If you were picking who might help a hurt Jewish man, most people would not pick a Samaritan. Not in a million years.

So the hurt man might have worried, “Oh no. Is he going to ignore me too? Or be mean?”

But Jesus says the Samaritan **saw** him—and his heart filled with **pity**. His heart went, “Oh! That poor man!” (That’s compassion—when you care so much inside that you do something about it.)

The Samaritan didn’t stand far away and stare. He hurried over and knelt down in the dust right next to him with a little *thump*.

“I’ve got you,” he might have said, with a kind voice, putting a gentle hand on the man’s shoulder.

He didn’t say, “Is this my problem?”  
He didn’t say, “What if I’m late?”  
He didn’t say, “You’re not my friend.”

He got to work.

He cleaned the man’s wounds. He poured oil and wine on them—like medicine that might sting a little, but helps them heal. He wrapped the wounds carefully, like tying a bandage with gentle fingers.

Then the Samaritan did something even harder. He lifted the hurt man onto his own animal. That means the hurt man got to ride… and the Samaritan had to walk.

Step after step, down the road they went.

The Samaritan brought him to an inn—a place to rest. Warm light in the windows. A safe bed inside. He stayed with him through the night. He made sure he had food and water. He checked on him again and again.

And in the morning, the Samaritan gave the innkeeper money.

“Please take care of him,” he said. “If it costs more, I’ll pay you when I come back.”

Then Jesus asked the people listening a question: “Which person was a neighbour to the man who got hurt?”

It wasn’t the priest.  
It wasn’t the Levite.  
It was the Samaritan—the one who showed mercy. The one who acted with kindness.

That’s why this story is so surprising and so important. The hero is not the person everyone expected. The hero is the person who **loved someone who was different**—someone he wasn’t “supposed” to like.

Not just for people in your class.  
Not just for people who look like you, talk like you, or like the same games.

**Kindness is for everyone.**

Help them pick up their things. Smile and say, “Do you want to be my partner?” Use your words and your feet and your hands to show, “You matter.”

Because being a Good Samaritan starts with one brave choice:

**Stop. Notice. Help.**

“Raise your hand if you’ve ever dropped your ice-cream on the ground and someone gave you theirs.  
Wow! That felt nice, didn’t it?  
Now, what if the person who helped you was someone you weren’t friends with—maybe even someone who’s been mean to you before? Would you be surprised? Today we’re going to hear a true story Jesus told about exactly that kind of surprise kindness.”

---

Imagine a dusty, hot road. The sun is sizzling like chips in a fryer. A man is walking from the town of Jericho to Jerusalem. Thieves jump out—BOOM!—they push him, take his money, rip his coat and rush away. The man is left lying on the ground, skinned knees, bruised face, too hurt to stand.

Along comes helper number one: a priest. The priest sees the hurt man, tiptoes around him and keeps walking.  
Next comes helper number two: a temple helper. He peeks, then hurries off.  
Both men were important, wore fancy clothes, knew lots of Bible verses—but they did zero helping.

Finally, along comes helper number three. He is from a place called Samaria. People in Jesus’ time thought, “Ugh, Samaritans—they’re different, they dress different, they talk different.” Jews and Samaritans usually ignored each other like smelly cheese. But this Samaritan man stops. He doesn’t just say, “Oh dear,” and stroll on. Listen to what he does:

- He sees.  
- His tummy hurts for the man—he feels.  
- He acts.  
  – Pours cool wine on the sore spots (it stings, but it cleans).  
  – Squishy olive oil next—like lotion on a sunburn.  
  – Tears his own scarf—rip!—and gently ties it around the wounds.  
  – Lifts the man onto his donkey, click-clop, clip-clop, all the way to an inn that smells of bread and hay.  
  – Stays the night, feeding soup.  
  – Next morning he pays the innkeeper two shiny coins. “If the bill is bigger, I’ll settle it when I come back,” he says. Then he waves goodbye.

Jesus looks at the people listening and asks, “Which one was a neighbour?”  
Everyone answers, “The one who helped!”  
Jesus smiles. “Go, do the same.”

---

Let’s press pause and think.  
The helper everyone expected to be nice—the priest—wasn’t.  
The helper no one expected—the outsider—was super-kind.  
That’s why Jesus loves this story. It flips expectations upside-down like a pancake.

Kindness isn’t just for our buddies.  
Kindness is for the new kid who wears different shoes.  
Kindness is for the big kid who accidentally bumps you.  
Kindness is for the grumpy neighbour who never smiles.  
God’s kindness has super-long arms—it reaches everyone.

---

So, how can we wear our “Good-Samaritan cap” this week?  
Here’s one simple mission you can do before next Sunday:

**THE BAND-AID CHALLENGE**  
1. Ask a grown-up for one plain band-aid.  
2. Stick it on your wrist or backpack strap—not for a real cut, just as a reminder.  
3. Every time you spot it, ask God, “Who needs help right now?”  
4. Then help: share a crayon, let someone go first, pick up the books someone spilled, smile at the lunch lady, invite the shy kid to play.  
5. When you get home, tell your family what you did. Maybe they’ll want a band-aid reminder too!

If we all do tiny helps, our school, playground and world will start to feel like one big safe inn where everyone belongs.

Let’s pray:  
“Jesus, thank You for the surprise Samaritan. Help us see, feel and act. Make us brave, kind kids who help everyone, not just our friends. Amen.”

Now, who’s ready for the Band-Aid Challenge? On the count of three, shout, “I’m in!”  
One… two… three…  
“I’M IN!”

“Who here has ever tripped on the playground, skinned a knee, and felt that big, hot tear coming?”  
Forty hands shoot up.  
“Great—because we’re about to race down a dusty road with a hurt man, two speedy walkers, and one surprise hero wearing a smile as wide as yours.”

So—open your ears, open your hearts, and imagine this:

One bright morning a teacher asked Jesus, “What must I do to live the best life?”  
Jesus smiled. “Love God with everything, and love your neighbor as yourself.”  
The teacher twirled his beard. “Sure, but… who exactly is my neighbor?”  
Jesus said, “Let me tell you a story.”

Picture a winding desert path between Jerusalem and Jericho. Rocks everywhere. Sun so bright it turns the sand white. A Jewish traveler whistles as he walks—until WHOOSH! Robbers jump out, rip his money bag, tear his shirt, and run. The man crumples, bloody and groaning.

Soon—clip-clop—here comes Priest #1, robe fluttering like a purple flag.  
The hurt man thinks, “Ah, rescue!”  
The priest looks, wrinkles his nose, swerves to the other side, and hurries on.  
Next—tap-tap—Levite #2 arrives, carrying temple music in his head.  
He peeks, gasps, and speed-walks away, sandals slapping like scared ducks.

Enter the surprise: clip-CLOP, clip-CLOP. A Samaritan rides up.  
Now, kids, here’s the twist: Jews and Samaritans were like two teams that never high-fived. They rolled their eyes at each other in the lunch line.  
But this Samaritan doesn’t roll anything except his sleeves.  
He jumps off his animal, knees scraping gravel.  
“Whoa, you’re hurt!” he says.  
He pours cool water on the wounds—drip, drop—like lemonade over ice.  
He wraps the cuts with soft cloth, gently, the way Mom ties your shoelaces double-knot-tight so you won’t fall again.  
Then he lifts the man onto his own donkey—hefty work!—and they sway to the nearest motel-inn.  
All night the Samaritan stays, spooning soup, wiping fever, paying the bill with his very last coins.  
“Keep the change,” he tells the owner. “If he needs more, I’ll pay when I return.”

Jesus looked at the teacher. “Which one was the neighbor?”  
The teacher whispered, “The one who showed kindness.”  
Jesus grinned. “Go, do the same.”

Why is this story huge?  
Because the helper was the last person anyone expected.  
Kindness didn’t wait for a matching jersey; it just leaped in and helped.

So—quick check:  
- Friends on your birthday list? Easy to be kind.  
- New kid who wears different shoes? Bigger chance to be amazing.  
- Sister who hogs the tablet? Super-size your heart.

Here’s a secret: kindness is like bubble solution. The more you blow, the more the air fills with shiny orbs that land on everyone. You can’t run out!

Your mission this week: be a Good-Samaritan-Kid.  
Look for one person outside your usual circle—someone sitting alone at lunch, someone who dropped crayons, someone who speaks a different language.  
Walk over, smile big, and do one helpful thing: share your cookie, pick up the crayons, say, “Want to play?”  
That’s it. One act. You’ll come home taller inside—promise!

Close your eyes. Hear the donkey hooves. Feel the desert wind.  
Now open your eyes: playground, hallway, living room—those are your roads.  
Travel them with wide-open kindness, and every bump becomes a chance to be the hero in someone’s story.

RXmTSId-oVZxzM5Lx8HfZ.text:
*Imagine you're at recess, and you see someone fall down and scrape their knee. They're sitting there crying, but everyone else just walks right past. Maybe they're not in your class. Maybe they dress differently. Maybe some kids whisper that they're "not cool." What would YOU do? Would you keep walking? Or would you stop?*

*Well, a long, long time ago, Jesus told a story about that exact question.*

*Picture this: A man was walking down a dangerous, winding road between Jerusalem and Jericho. The sun beat down hot. Dust swirled in his face. He could smell the dirt and hear the rocks crunching under his sandals. Suddenly—BAM!—robbers jumped out from behind the rocks! They stole his money, his bag, his sandals, everything! And they left him lying by the side of the road, all bruised and bloody. Ouch! He could barely move.*

*Soon, a priest came walking by. This was someone who worked at the temple and prayed all day long! Everyone thought he was super holy. The hurt man probably thought, "Oh good, he'll help me!" But do you know what the priest did? He saw the man, looked away really fast, and hurried to the other side of the road. His long robes swished as he rushed past. He kept walking! Maybe he thought, "I'm too busy. Someone else will help."*

*Then a Levite came by—another important church helper. He walked right past too! He probably thought, "This is messy. I don't want to get involved."*

*But then... a Samaritan came traveling down the road. Now, here's what you need to know. Samaritans and Jews were like kids from two schools that were HUGE rivals. They didn't talk to each other. They didn't eat together. Some people said mean things about each other. They were supposed to be enemies.*

*But when the Samaritan saw the hurt man, he didn't see an enemy. He just saw someone who needed help. His heart went, "Oh no! You poor thing!"*

*He got down on his knees right there in the dirt. Can you imagine? He gently poured oil and wine on the wounds—it probably stung, but it cleaned them. He wrapped soft cloth bandages around the cuts. The man groaned, and the Samaritan whispered, "Shhh, it's okay. I've got you." Then, very carefully, he lifted the man onto his own donkey and walked slowly, step by step, to an inn, holding him steady so he wouldn't fall off. All night long, he stayed up, giving him water, wiping his forehead, making sure he was okay. The next morning, he took out his own money, gave it to the innkeeper, and said, "Take good care of him. Give him food and a soft bed. I'll come back and pay for everything—whatever it costs."*

*Jesus asked, "Which one was a good neighbor?" The answer was obvious!*

*The surprising part is that the two religious leaders missed the point completely. They thought loving God was just about saying prayers and following rules. But the Samaritan showed that loving God means loving people—especially when it's hard, especially when they're different, especially when no one else will.*

*So here's your mission for this week: Be a Good Samaritan. Look for ONE person who seems left out. Maybe at lunch, someone is sitting alone at a table. Maybe at recess, someone is standing by the fence, just watching. Walk over and say, "Hi! Want to sit with me?" or "Want to join our game?"*

*It might feel a little scary. It might be inconvenient. But that's what makes you brave and kind—just like the Good Samaritan.*

*Who will you help this week? Keep your eyes open. Be the one who stops. Because you never know when your kindness will be exactly what someone needs.*

hRcKmQUbqvg85vTvW1mJC.text:
*What would you do if you saw someone sitting all alone at lunch?*

Maybe you’d walk right over and ask to join them. Or maybe you’d feel a little shy and keep walking. Or maybe—and be honest here—maybe you’d think, “That kid is weird,” and you’d keep your distance.

Well, today I’m going to tell you a story Jesus told about a man who had that exact same choice. And what he did was so surprising, so upside-down, that people are still talking about it 2,000 years later!

Here’s how it starts:

A man was walking down a long, dusty road. The sun was blazing hot. Sweat dripped down his face. His feet were sore. Then—BAM! Robbers jumped out! They took his money, his bag, his nice sandals, and left him lying in the dirt. He was hurt. Badly. He couldn’t even stand up.

Soon, a priest came walking by. This was a church helper, someone who prayed a lot! The hurt man thought, *Oh good, I’m saved!* But the priest saw him, made a face, and hurried to the other side of the road. He kept walking.

Then a Levite came—another important church guy. He saw the hurt man too. He even paused for a second. But then he shook his head and kept going. *Not my problem.*

Now here’s where it gets wild.

A third man came along. A Samaritan. And when the children listening to Jesus heard this, they probably went, “Ewww, a Samaritan?” Because back then, Jewish people and Samaritan people did NOT get along. They were neighbors who acted like enemies. They didn’t eat together. They didn’t talk to each other. They thought they were better than each other.

But this Samaritan man? He saw the hurt traveler and his heart went *THUMP*. He ran over. “Oh no! Are you okay?” He poured oil and wine on the wounds to clean them—*ouch, ouch, it’s okay, I’m helping!* He wrapped bandages around them. He lifted the man onto his own donkey and walked beside him, holding him steady. When they got to an inn, he stayed up all night caring for him.

The next morning, he gave the innkeeper money. “Take care of him. Whatever you spend, I’ll pay you back when I return.”

Then Jesus asked the people listening: “Who was a good neighbor?”

Everyone knew the answer. “The one who showed kindness!”

But here’s the twist: Jesus was saying that being a neighbor isn’t about where you live. It’s about how you *show up* for people—especially people who are different from you, or that others ignore, or that you might not even like!

The Samaritan could’ve thought, “That guy’s probably rude to Samaritans. He deserves what he got.” But he didn’t. He saw someone hurting and he helped. He used his hands, his time, his money, his donkey—he used everything he had!

So what does this mean for us?

It means kindness isn’t just for your best friends. It’s for the new kid who talks differently. It’s for the person who sits alone. It’s for the kid who bumped into you yesterday and didn’t say sorry. It’s for *everyone*.

Jesus is basically saying: “I don’t care who started it. I care who *helps*.”

This week, I want you to be a Good Samaritan. Just once. Find one person who seems left out or different. Maybe they’re new. Maybe they’re quiet. Maybe they’re not in your friend group.

Then do ONE thing:

- Invite them to play at recess
- Share your snack
- Ask them about their favorite video game
- Give them a real smile and a “hello”
- Save them a seat

It doesn’t have to be huge. The Samaritan just started with stopping. You can start with stopping too.

Because here’s the secret: when you’re kind to the person everyone else walks past, you’re walking the exact same road Jesus walked. And that road? It’s the best road there is.

So—who will you be a Good Samaritan to this week?

Imagine you’re at recess, building the world’s tallest sandcastle. You’ve got the perfect bucket, the best spot, and then—BAM! Someone you don’t really know trips and crashes right into it. Your castle is ruined. They’re crying. What do you do? Do you help them, even though they’re not your friend? Or do you walk away?

That’s exactly the kind of question Jesus wanted people to think about. And he told an amazing story to help. It’s called the parable of the Good Samaritan. Let me paint it for you.

Picture this: a long, dusty road winding through rocky hills. The sun is baking hot. A man is walking alone when suddenly—ROBBERS! They jump out, steal everything he has, even his shoes, and leave him bruised and bleeding by the side of the road.

Soon, a priest comes along. Now, this is someone important—like a principal, but for the temple. You’d think he’d stop, right? But he looks at the hurt man, and… he crosses to the other side. He keeps walking.

Next, another temple helper called a Levite walks by. He sees the man too. He even slows down! But then he shakes his head and hurries past.

Here’s where the story gets surprising. The next person coming down the road is a Samaritan. Now, kids, you need to know something: Samaritans and the hurt man were NOT friends. They were more like rivals—like two teams who never, ever root for each other. They had different traditions, and they’d been arguing for years. If anyone was going to walk past, it should be the Samaritan, right?

But he doesn’t.

The Samaritan sees the hurt man and his heart does a little *flip*. He runs over, kneels in the dust, and gets right to work. He pours wine on the wounds to clean them—ouch!—and smooths on oil to soothe them. He wraps bandages around the cuts. Then—get this—he lifts the man onto his own donkey and walks, sweating and tired, all the way to an inn. He carries the man inside like a sleeping child.

“Take care of him,” the Samaritan tells the innkeeper, and he hands over his own money. “If he needs more, I’ll pay you when I come back.”

Just like that. No questions about who the man was. No “but he’s not my friend!” No “what if I’m late?” Just kindness. Pure, bold, sweaty, expensive kindness.

Jesus looked at the people listening and asked, “Who was the neighbor?”

Everyone knew. The neighbor wasn’t the important priest. It wasn’t the busy Levite. It was the one who showed kindness, even though it was hard, even though they were supposed to be enemies.

And here’s the big lesson for us: **Everyone is your neighbor.** Not just your best buddy. Not just the kids in your class who like the same stuff. Not just the people who are easy to be nice to. The kid who sits alone at lunch? Neighbor. The person who always wins the game you wanted to win? Neighbor. The kid who looks different, talks different, or thinks different? Neighbor.

Being a Good Samaritan doesn’t mean you need a donkey and bandages. It means you see someone hurting, or left out, or just having a rotten day—and you don’t walk to the other side. You stop.

This week, I want you to try one thing. Just one. Look around. Find someone who might feel like they’re lying in the dust—even if it’s just dust from a bad day. Maybe they dropped their books. Maybe they look lonely. Maybe they need a partner for a game.

Be their Samaritan. Walk over. Say, “Need help?” That’s it. That’s the whole thing.

Because kindness? It doesn’t have a “but.” It just has a “yes.”

And you—you’ve got more “yes” in you than you know.

Let me show you what happened.

Picture a road baked by the sun, curling through rocky hills. A man is walking home when—out of nowhere—robbers attack. They steal his money, his bag, even his shoes. They leave him bleeding in the dirt.

Soon, a priest comes along. This is someone important, a church leader. You’d think he’d stop, right? He doesn’t even slow down. He just... crosses to the other side and keeps walking.

Next, a Levite walks by. That’s another temple helper. He slows down. He looks. But then he shakes his head and hurries past.

Now here’s the twist. The next person is a Samaritan. And back then, Samaritans and this hurt man were enemies. Not just “we-don’t-get-along” enemies—more like two teams who have hated each other for generations. They disagreed about everything. They didn’t share food. They didn’t pray together. They’d walk extra miles just to avoid each other’s towns.

If anyone was going to keep walking, it should be the Samaritan.

But he doesn’t.

He sees the hurt man and his chest tightens. He runs over, kneels in the dust, and gets to work. He pours wine on the wounds—it stings, but it cleans. He pours oil on them next—it soothes. He wraps cloth around the cuts, tying gentle knots. Then he lifts the man onto his own donkey and walks, sweating in the heat, mile after mile, all the way to an inn. He carries him inside like a sleeping child and lays him on a bed.

“Take care of him,” the Samaritan tells the innkeeper, and he hands over two silver coins. That’s two days’ wages. “If it costs more, I’ll pay you when I come back.”

Just like that. No questions about where the man was from. No “but he’s not my friend!” No “what if I’m late for dinner?” Just kindness. The kind that costs time, costs money, costs pride.

Jesus asked the people listening, “Who was the neighbor?”

Everyone knew. The neighbor wasn’t the important priest. It wasn’t the busy Levite. It was the one who showed mercy, even though it was hard, even though they were supposed to be enemies.

The new kid who doesn’t know anyone yet? Neighbor. The kid who always wins the game you want to win? Neighbor. The kid who eats different food at lunch, or wears different clothes, or just seems... different? Neighbor. Even the kid who was mean to you yesterday? Still neighbor.

Being a Good Samaritan doesn’t mean you need a donkey and bandages. It means you notice when someone is hurting, or left out, or just having a rotten day—and you don’t walk to the other side. You stop.

Maybe you see someone who dropped their books in the hallway. Everyone’s walking past. You stop and help pick them up.

Maybe you see someone standing alone at recess, kicking the dirt. You walk over and ask, “Want to play?”

Maybe you hear someone getting teased, and everyone else is laughing. You don’t join in. You don’t walk away. You say, “Hey, that’s not cool,” or you check on the kid later.

This week, try one thing. Just one. Keep your eyes open. Find someone who might feel like they’re lying in the dust—even if it’s just dust from a bad day. Walk over. Say, “Need help?” or “Want to sit with me?” That’s it. That’s the whole thing.

Because kindness isn’t about waiting for the perfect person to help. It’s about seeing the person right in front of you.

And you? You’ve got exactly what it takes to be the one who stops.

*What if I told you that being a hero doesn’t mean wearing a cape or having super strength? What if I told you that you could be a hero just by choosing to be kind to someone everyone else ignores?*

Let me tell you a story Jesus once told.

One day, a man was walking down a twisty, dusty road from Jerusalem to Jericho. It was hot. The rocks were sharp. And WHAM! Out jumped some robbers—they took his money, tore his clothes, and left him bruised and bleeding on the side of the road.

Soon, a priest came walking by. A priest! That’s like a super-important church leader. The hurt man probably thought, *Yes! I’m saved!* But the priest looked at him, then looked away, and kept walking. Right past.

Next came a Levite—another big-deal helper at the temple. He saw the man too. He even slowed down. But then he hurried away. Nope. Not stopping.

Now here’s where the story gets surprising. Along came a Samaritan. But wait—Jesus’s friends *hated* Samaritans. The two groups argued all the time, like rival soccer teams who booed each other at every game. If you were Jewish, you didn’t talk to Samaritans. You crossed the street to avoid them.

But this Samaritan? He stopped.

He saw the blood. He saw the pain. And his heart did a little *ouch* inside. He didn’t check to see if the man was “on his team.” He just saw a person who needed help.

He poured olive oil and wine on the wounds—*ssssst*—to clean them. He wrapped bandages around them. Then—get this—he lifted the man onto his own donkey, which meant *he* had to walk. He clop-clop-clopped to an inn, carried the man to a bed like a sleeping child, and stayed up all night caring for him.

In the morning, he gave the innkeeper money. “Take care of him,” he said. “If it costs more, I’ll pay you back when I return.”

Wow.

Later, Jesus asked, “Who was a neighbor to the hurt man?”

Everyone knew the answer. “The one who showed kindness!”

“Then go and do like he did,” Jesus said.

So here’s what this means for you: Kindness doesn’t have a sign that says “Friends Only.” It doesn’t check to see if someone is cool enough, or in your class, or wears the right shoes. Kindness just *acts*.

This week, I want you to be a Good Samaritan. Just once. Look around at recess or in the lunchroom. Find the kid who’s standing alone. The one nobody’s talking to. Maybe they’re new. Maybe they’re just having a rough day.

Walk up. Smile. Ask, “Want to play with us?” or “Can I sit with you?”

That’s it. That’s your superpower.

You don’t need a cape. You just need to notice someone others are walking past—and choose to stop.

**Who will you be a Good Samaritan to this week?**

Let’s go be heroes.

**The Superhero in the Ditch**

*Have you ever seen someone fall down at the playground? Maybe they scraped their knee. Maybe they dropped their lunch tray and spaghetti went *everywhere*. What do you usually do?*

*Do you walk past? Or do you stop?*

Today I want to tell you about the most surprising superhero in the whole Bible. He didn't wear a cape. He didn't have super strength. But he did something so brave, so kind, that people are still talking about him two thousand years later.

---

Once upon a time, a man was walking down a steep, twisty road. The sun beat down. Rocks crunched under his sandals. This road was dangerous—like a dark alley behind a grocery store, but with robbers hiding behind big boulders instead of dumpsters.

*Suddenly—BAM!*

Three mean men jumped out. They grabbed the traveler. They took his money, his coat, even his shoes. Then they hurt him—*badly*—and left him bleeding in the dirt.

The man couldn't move. His head throbbed. His side ached. Flies buzzed around him. He was alone, hurting, and helpless.

Then—*clip-clop, clip-clop*—hoofbeats!

A priest came riding by. This was a *church leader*. Someone who prayed every day. Someone who taught other people how to love God.

The hurt man tried to call out. "Help... please..."

The priest looked down. He saw the blood. He saw the bruises. And he—*swerved his donkey to the other side of the road*—and kept going.

*Clip-clop, clip-clop, clip-clop...* Gone.

The hurt man closed his eyes. The sun got hotter.

Then—*clip-clop, clip-clop*—more hoofbeats!

A Levite came by. This was a *temple helper*. Someone who worked at church every single day. Someone who knew all the rules about being good.

The hurt man tried again. "Please... water..."

The Levite slowed down. He looked. He even walked closer. But then he wrinkled his nose, held his breath, and—*swerved to the other side*—and kept going.

*Clip-clop, clip-clop, clip-clop...* Gone.

The hurt man felt tears mixing with the dust on his face. No one was going to stop. He might die right there.

Then—*clip-clop, clip-clop*—one more traveler.

But this one was different.

This man was a *Samaritan*. Now, here's the surprising part: Samaritans and the hurt man's people? They were *enemies*. Like rival sports teams, but worse. They didn't eat together. They didn't play together. They definitely didn't *help* each other.

The Samaritan saw the man in the ditch. And he didn't swerve. He *stopped*.

He climbed down from his donkey. His knees hit the dirt. He touched the stranger's bloody forehead. He poured stinging wine on the wounds to clean them—*ouch!*—and soft oil to help them heal. He ripped his own shirt to make bandages.

Then he lifted the hurt man—*heavy, groaning, smelly*—onto his own donkey. The Samaritan walked beside him, holding him steady, for *miles*.

They reached a hotel. The Samaritan carried the man inside. He tucked him into bed. He stayed all night, making sure the hurt man was breathing, bringing him water, wiping his forehead.

Next morning, the Samaritan had to leave. But he pulled out his money—*real silver coins*—and pressed them into the innkeeper's hand. "Take care of him," he said. "If it costs more, I'll pay you when I come back."

*He didn't even know this man's name.*

---

Now, why is this story so surprising?

The priest and Levite? Everyone expected *them* to help. They were the "good guys." But they were too busy, too grossed out, too scared.

The Samaritan? Everyone expected him to walk right past. He had *every excuse*. Wrong team. Wrong neighborhood. Not his problem.

But he saw a hurt human being. And his heart went *boom*—like a superhero signal lighting up the sky.

Jesus told this story to answer one big question: "Who is my neighbor?" His answer? *Everyone.* The person who looks different. The person you don't understand. The person who might not even say thank you.

---

So here's your mission this week, superheroes-in-training:

**Find one person who needs help—and be the one who stops.**

Maybe it's the new kid standing alone at recess. Maybe it's your little brother when he drops his Lego tower. Maybe it's someone who was mean to you yesterday—*especially* then.

You don't need money. You don't need a donkey. You just need to notice, and care, and *do something*.

The world is full of people swerving to the other side. Be the one who stops.

*Who's ready?*

He lay there, hot and hurting. The sun got higher. No one came.

Soon, *clip-clop, clip-clop*—a priest came walking by. He wore fancy robes and worked at the temple. He saw the hurt man. He probably thought, *“Yikes, that looks messy.”* So he crossed to the other side of the road. *Zoom!* Kept walking.

**The Superhero in the Ditch**

"Hey—quick! What would you do if you saw someone fall off their bike in the playground? And they scraped their knee *really* badly. And—this is the tricky part—it was someone who never lets YOU join their games?"

*Pause. Look around. Let hands shoot up.*

Some of you are thinking, "I'd help!" Some of you are thinking, "Hmm, maybe I'd walk the other way." And some of you are thinking, "They never helped ME."

That's exactly what happened in the most surprising story Jesus ever told.

---

Once upon a time—*and this really happened*—a man was walking down a steep, twisty road between two cities. The sun beat down. His sandals kicked up dust. Suddenly—*BAM!*—robbers jumped out! They grabbed his bag, they grabbed his coat, they even grabbed his shoes. And they left him lying in the dirt, bleeding and groaning, half-dead.

*Can you picture him? Shivering even though it's hot. Too hurt to stand up. Alone.*

Then—*clip-clop, clip-clop*—someone came riding by on a donkey. It was a priest! That's like a really important church helper. The hurt man thought, "Saved!" But the priest looked down... *looked away*... and kept walking. *Clip-clop, clip-clop,* gone.

*Can you believe it?*

Then—*clip-clop, clip-clop*—another donkey! This time it was a Levite, another special helper in church. He slowed down. He looked. He even *almost* stopped. But then—*clip-clop, clip-clop*—he kept going too.

Two helpers. Zero help.

---

But then—*thump-thump-thump*—came different footsteps. Slower. A man walking, not riding. And when THIS man saw the hurt person, he STOPPED. Dead stop.

Now here's the SHOCKING part. This man was a Samaritan. And back then, Samaritans and the hurt man? They were ENEMIES. Like, "you're-not-invited-to-my-birthday-party" times a thousand. They didn't wave at each other. They didn't eat at the same tables. They definitely didn't HELP each other.

But this Samaritan? He knelt right down in the dirt. He touched the bleeding places—*gently, gently*—and poured wine on them (which stings!) and oil (which soothes). He ripped his own shirt to make bandages. He lifted the hurt man onto his own donkey—*ugh, heavy!*—and walked beside him, sweating, for miles.

At the inn, he didn't dump the man and run. He stayed up all night, making sure he was okay. And in the morning, he pulled out his money—*real coins, clinking*—and said to the innkeeper: "Take care of him. If it costs more, I'll pay when I come back."

*He came back?* He CAME BACK.

---

Jesus asked the people listening: "Which one was a neighbour?"

And they had to admit: "The one who showed kindness."

Not the fancy priest. Not the important Levite. The one they didn't even LIKE.

Here's the secret Jesus was teaching: **Kindness is a superpower you can use on ANYONE.** Not just your best friend. Not just the kid who's nice to you. Not just people who look like you or talk like you or believe what you believe.

The Samaritan had EVERY reason to keep walking. But he looked at that hurt person and thought: "He's a person. He needs help. That's enough."

---

So this week, I want you to try something. I call it **"Samaritan Eyes."**

Look around your playground, your classroom, your bus. Find someone who needs help—maybe someone who's dropped their books, or sitting alone at lunch, or crying in the corner. And here's the hard part: maybe it's someone who hasn't been kind to YOU.

Then? Be the one who stops. Be the one who helps. Be the one who comes back.

You don't need a donkey. You don't need money. You just need to notice, and care, and *do something.*

Who's ready to be a superhero in sneakers?

*Me too. Let's go.*

**The Superhero Nobody Expected**

"Quick—raise your hand if you've ever fallen down and scraped your knee!"

---

**The Dangerous Road**

Imagine a winding dirt road, all rocky and steep, curling down between brown hills like a snake. The sun's blazing hot. Dust everywhere—*pfft pfft*—in your mouth, in your eyes.

A man was walking this road. Nice guy. Had his bag, his water, probably thinking about what he'd make for dinner. Then—*BAM!*—robbers jumped out from behind the rocks! They grabbed his bag, they grabbed his coat, they even grabbed his shoes. And they hurt him. Badly.

They left him there. Half-dressed. Bleeding. *Barely breathing.*

---

**The Parade of "Busy"**

Along came a priest. Fancy robes, important job, knows ALL the rules about being good. He sees the hurt man. He *crosses to the other side of the road.* Keeps walking. *Clip clop, clip clop.* Gone.

Then—here comes a helper from the temple! This guy's WHOLE JOB is about God and doing right. He looks... he slows down... he *crosses over too.* *Clip clop, clip clop.* Also gone.

Two good people. Two people who should DEFINITELY help. And they didn't.

---

**The Surprise Hero**

Now here comes the twist.

A Samaritan man. *Samaritan.* 

Here's the thing—and this is SUPER important—Samaritans and the hurt man's people? They did NOT get along. At all. Imagine if your football team and your rival football team had been fighting for a hundred years. That's them. If they saw each other in the street, they'd probably stick their tongues out. What would you do?

Today I want to tell you about a story from the Bible—a true story—that shows us exactly what it looks like to be a helper. It's about a man who made a choice. And I think it'll surprise you.

---

**The Story**

A long, long time ago, in a land where the sun was hot and the roads were dusty, a man was walking alone. He wasn't walking to school or to a friend's house. He was traveling far away from everyone he knew.

Suddenly—out of nowhere—some bad men jumped out! They beat him up, took his money, and left him lying on the ground. He couldn't move. He couldn't call for help. He was hurt, scared, and all alone.

Now, pretty soon, a priest came walking down that same road. You know what a priest is? He was someone who worked at the church, someone who taught people about God.

The priest saw the hurt man lying there. He looked at him. And then... he walked to the other side of the road and kept going. He didn't stop. He didn't help.

A little while later, a helper from the church came by. He saw the man too. But he also walked right past.

Can you imagine how that hurt man felt? Lying there in the dirt, in pain, watching person after person walk by like he wasn't even there?

Then... a third person came along. He was riding a donkey—kind of like a horse, but smaller. And when he saw the hurt man, he *stopped*.

This man was a Samaritan.

That's what kindness looks like.

---
